issues.title: Windows desktop: repeated canceled branch-diff-stats leaves active Git children consuming CPU and memory

labels.name: bug
labels.description: Something isn't working

labels.name: windows-os
labels.description: Issues related to Codex on Windows systems

labels.name: app
labels.description: Issues related to the Codex desktop app

issues.body:
### What version of the Codex App are you using (From "About Codex" dialog)?

Observed Windows package: `OpenAI.Codex_26.1027.3384.0_x64`.
Desktop runtime logs report release `26.1027.30824`.
These values were collected from the running process and logs, rather than the About dialog.

### What subscription do you have?

Not collected for this report.

### What platform is your computer?

Windows x64, `Microsoft Windows NT 10.0.26200.0`; approximately 32 GiB RAM and 32 logical processors.

### What issue are you seeing?

Codex Desktop repeatedly starts and cancels the same expensive branch-diff statistics request in a large local Unity repository. Real Git for Windows children remain running after their launcher parent processes have exited, and multiple comparisons overlap with substantial CPU and memory use.

Read-only diagnostics on 2026-10-31 found:

- Between 18:41:04 and 18:52:15 UTC, the desktop Git-worker log contained **150** matching `git.command.complete` records. All 150 reported `aborted=true`, `failureReason=canceled`, `success=false`, `requestKind=branch-diff-stats`, and `source=review_model`. Recorded durations ranged from 10 to 21,353 ms.
- All requests compared the current checkout with the same older commit. That commit is both local `master` and `origin/master`; `origin/HEAD` points to `origin/master`. The active branch was `development`, 234 commits beyond that July 29 base, with approximately 6,960 changed paths. The comparison includes large binary assets, including approximately 580 MiB archives and 64 MiB textures.
- Process enumeration captured the desktop `ChatGPT.exe` NodeService worker launching `Git/cmd/git.exe`, which launches `Git/mingw64/bin/git.exe` with the same diff arguments.
- A later snapshot contained seven real matching Git workers plus one launcher. Several real workers had recorded parent PIDs that no longer existed. Their accumulated CPU time was increasing; these were working processes, rather than zero-work processes wedged before Git main().
- In one 12-second sample, two matching workers each consumed approximately one logical CPU core. Individual workers reached roughly 2.6-3.4 GiB working sets. Working sets include shared/mapped pages and must not be summed as unique RAM. At one snapshot, combined private committed memory for the matching Git processes was approximately 1.9 GiB.

Sanitized command shape:

```text
git -c diff.mnemonicPrefix=false -c diff.noprefix=false -c core.quotePath=false -c safe.bareRepository=explicit -c core.hooksPath=NUL -c core.fsmonitor= diff --no-ext-diff --no-textconv --color=never --src-prefix=a/ --dst-prefix=b/ <old-master-commit> --find-renames --raw --no-abbrev --numstat -z
```

Representative sanitized log fields:

```text
aborted=true exitCode=null failureReason=canceled
requestKind=branch-diff-stats source=review_model
subcommand=diff success=false timedOut=false outputLimitExceeded=false
```

This is consistent with redundant refresh/cancellation and incomplete descendant cleanup, but the exact internal trigger and root cause have not been established.

### What steps can reproduce the bug?

No deterministic minimal reproducer yet. Observed conditions:

1. Use Codex Desktop on Windows with Git for Windows and a large, existing Unity repository containing tracked binary assets.
2. Work on a development branch whose default remote branch remains several months and hundreds of commits behind.
3. During ordinary desktop use, allow the repository/review metadata to refresh. The worker logs identify the affected operation as `branch-diff-stats`; the exact UI action that begins the loop has not been isolated.
4. Observe repeated cancellations for the same base commit, overlapping real Git workers, and some real children continuing after their launcher parent exits.

No deliberate stress reproduction, process termination, repository rewriting, or application patching was performed during diagnosis. Switching the review scope to Unstaged was suggested as a workaround but has not been validated.

### What is the expected behavior?

Coalesce equivalent branch-stat refreshes and bound concurrent comparisons per repository. Cancellation should clean up the actual Git process tree, including the real Git child behind the Windows launcher. Avoid repeatedly restarting an expensive unchanged comparison before earlier children have stopped; retain/cache results where appropriate and make expensive background work visible.

### Additional information

Related reports: #54497 (Windows Git process fan-out/resource exhaustion), #30820 (desktop review metadata refresh costs), and #41783 (Windows Git launcher/grandchild cleanup).

This report records the narrower `branch-diff-stats` cancellation pattern with active, CPU-consuming children. It does not establish that those reports have the same root cause. In particular, the zero-work/pre-main hang described in #41783 does not match the active CPU counters observed here.

The report excludes project names, local filesystem paths, usernames, repository URLs, commit hashes, chat/session IDs, credentials, source code, and raw log attachments. Only sanitized diagnostics are included.

issues.title: [App] Add Insert/Send mode for desktop dictation hotkeys (no Codex Micro required)

labels.name: enhancement
labels.description: New feature or request

labels.name: app
labels.description: Issues related to the Codex desktop app

issues.body:
## Reviewer decision requested

Please choose one outcome for this Desktop behavior contract:

- **Accept:** invite or port the private Desktop implementation.
- **Adjust:** identify the behavior, copy, or safety constraint to change.
- **Decline:** close the proposal without requiring an implementation review.

A proposal-only commit and visual are ready to port, but upstream PR creation is permission-gated by the repository's invitation-only contribution policy. This issue is therefore structured as the review surface.

- **Proposal commit:** [daeshawnballard/codex@bcfef48](https://github.com/daeshawnballard/codex/commit/bcfef48b1bfe6639ae80fa2e78f8c7922856c025)
- **Full design packet:** [behavior matrix, flow, implementation sketch, and tests](https://github.com/daeshawnballard/codex/blob/bcfef48b1bfe6639ae80fa2e78f8c7922856c025/.github/design-proposals/desktop-dictation-hotkey-completion.md)

## What

Add an **After transcription** setting for both Desktop dictation hotkeys:

- **Insert** (default) — transcribe into the Codex composer without submitting.
- **Send** — transcribe and submit a successful, non-empty transcript through the ordinary composer path.

After **Send**, the existing Queue/Steer preference remains authoritative. Dictation targeting another application always remains insert-only; this feature must never synthesize Enter or submit an external form or message.

## Why

Voice-first workflows currently require a manual send action after every hotkey transcription. Keeping **Insert** as the default preserves today's review-first workflow, while **Send** removes that repeated action for users who explicitly opt in.

## Proposed settings UI

![Codex Desktop Dictation settings with a new After transcription Insert or Send control](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/daeshawnballard/codex/bcfef48b1bfe6639ae80fa2e78f8c7922856c025/.github/design-proposals/assets/desktop-dictation-hotkey-completion-settings.png)

The mockup selects **Send** to make the new state visible; the shipped default should be **Insert**.

## Behavior contract

| Context | Setting | Result |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Cursor is outside Codex | Either | Insert transcript at the cursor; never submit |
| Codex composer | Insert | Insert transcript and keep the draft editable |
| Codex composer, no active turn | Send | Submit through the standard composer path and start a turn |
| Codex composer, active turn | Send + Queue | Submit normally and queue the prompt |
| Codex composer, active turn | Send + Steer | Submit normally and steer the active turn |
| Empty, cancelled, or failed transcription | Either | Do not insert or send |

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    H["Dictation hotkey stops"] --> T["Transcription succeeds"]
    T --> A{"Codex composer?"}
    A -- "No" --> I["Insert only"]
    A -- "Yes" --> P{"After transcription"}
    P -- "Insert (default)" --> I
    P -- "Send" --> S["Standard composer submit"]
    S --> R{"Turn running?"}
    R -- "No" --> Start["Start turn"]
    R -- "Yes + Queue" --> Queue["Queue prompt"]
    R -- "Yes + Steer" --> Steer["Steer active turn"]
```

## How

The shipped app already exposes separate **Stop dictation** and **Transcribe and send** actions. The in-app hotkey completion path currently selects the insert action. The smallest private Desktop change is to persist one app-owned preference and choose the existing completion action at that boundary:

```ts
const action =
  target.kind === "codex-composer"
    ? settings.dictationHotkeyCompletion
    : "insert";

stopDictation(action);
```

The preference should stay in the existing opaque `desktop.*` namespace, defaulting to `"insert"`. No new app-server setting type or `turn/queue` RPC is needed. **Send** should invoke the same composer submission function as the send button so draft handling, Queue/Steer routing, accessibility behavior, analytics, and dictation submit-source metadata do not fork.

## Acceptance tests

- An absent preference resolves to **Insert**; both values persist across restart.
- Hold-to-dictate and toggle dictation honor the selected action exactly once per recording session.
- **Insert** leaves the Codex transcript editable.
- **Send** starts a turn while idle and follows Queue/Steer during an active turn.
- Dictation targeting another application always inserts and never submits.
- Empty, cancelled, failed, and retried transcriptions never cause a send.
- Existing composer content is handled identically to a send-button submission.

## Risks and non-goals

- Defaulting to **Insert** prevents a migration surprise.
- External targets fail closed to insert, preventing accidental submission.
- One terminal action per recording session prevents duplicate sends.
- Voice chat is unchanged.
- Transcription-engine latency is a separate concern; this proposal changes completion behavior only.

## Related issue

#37321 requests send-on-release for Codex Micro push-to-talk. This proposal is broader: it covers both Desktop hold/toggle dictation hotkeys, makes Insert/Send an explicit setting, preserves Queue/Steer routing, and defines external-app safety. The two can share the same underlying composer submission behavior without treating either report as redundant.

cc @thsottiaux

- macOS, dots-managed cloud work, GitHub integration, and delegated execution on the connected Mac.
- GitHub CLI: 2.101.0. Exact Codex/client/backend builds are unknown.

Incident timeline (reconstructed; not a deterministic minimal reproduction):

1. October 3: The user initially received rejection reports without an actionable explanation or recovery path. We cannot establish whether the underlying reason was absent or inadequately surfaced. Later diagnostic evidence contained a public-source-upload refusal stating that approval did not unambiguously cover the exact payload and destination, despite an explicit public-exposure explanation and the user's subsequent instruction to proceed. Repository ownership and push access were independently verified. Exact original invocation timestamps and request IDs were unavailable.

2. The user subsequently published the prepared source from another independently operated Mac session. The resulting source tree matched the prepared files. A later PR creation through dots and CI reads succeeded. This rules out a blanket inability to access or write to GitHub, but is not a controlled same-session comparison.

3. In a separate private-repository development workflow, tree creation and a PR-review request were denied with explanations citing the read-only reporting restriction and no later authorization. The user had directly requested development to resume after the reporting task.

4. October 4, around 01:48 UTC: A previously rejected second tree-upload batch succeeded after renewed user instructions. Batches 3–10 then succeeded. Batch 11 was denied on read-only-scope grounds. Its retry was denied on additional grounds of a large private source upload to an unverified destination. Prior read-only checks had verified repository identity, ownership and private visibility.

5. Around 01:53 UTC: The assistant asked specifically about uploading the reviewed source/tests to that private repository and creating a draft PR with CI, separately from the read-only report. The user approved. Batch 11 and commit creation then succeeded, with remote source-tree verification.

6. Around 01:55 UTC: The subsequent branch-creation call returned “user cancelled MCP tool call”. At 02:15 UTC, the user explicitly stated they had not cancelled anything. The actual cancellation source is unknown. This is distinct from another long-running call the coordinating assistant intentionally interrupted.

7. At the user's request, the workflow moved to gh CLI on the connected Mac. Read-only authentication/repository checks succeeded. Branch creation was still rejected before command execution, citing the original read-only scope and treating forwarded later approval as insufficiently attributable. One retry with the original question and user response was also denied. No branch, draft PR or CI run resulted for this private-repository candidate.

Expected behavior:
Evaluate each action using attributable current user authorization and the scope of the applicable task, while preserving safety restrictions. When approval is insufficient, identify precisely what is missing and provide a supported recovery path. Expose useful diagnostic references and distinguish user cancellation from other interruptions.

Limits:
Different batches contain different payloads, so their differing outcomes do not prove nondeterminism for identical inputs. We have not established a single root cause, a GitHub permission defect, or a payload-size limit. The CLI write failures described above occurred before the command ran; they were not errors returned by gh or GitHub.

issues.body:
### What version of the Codex App are you using?

- Codex Desktop version: `26.721.31836`
- Release date shown in the app: July 23, 2026
- Build branding shown in the app: Powered by Codex & OWL

### What subscription do you have?

ChatGPT Pro — the $200/month plan.

### What platform is your computer?

MacBook Pro with 16 GB of memory. The exact macOS version was not captured.

### Model and context state at the time of failure

- Model: GPT-5.6 Sol
- Reasoning settings used during the long-running thread: **Extra High → High → Medium**
- The 93% context screenshot was captured while Medium reasoning was selected
- Context window: 93% full
- Tokens used: 240k / 258k
- Primary Codex `/feedback` Session ID: `019f5be9-903c-7fd0-a8c9-5014bccc05b8`

### Summary

A long-running project chat entered a context auto-compaction loop. After each `Context automatically compacted` event, Codex retained the broad project objective but appeared to lose its execution progress.

It repeatedly:

1. reread the same files;
2. reloaded the same skills or memory files;
3. restated that it had found the exact defect;
4. promised that the next update would contain the completed change;
5. compacted context again before completing the edit;
6. restarted the same analysis and file-reading cycle.

The requested implementation was not completed, the useful project-chat context became difficult to recover, and the repeated loop consumed roughly 10%–15% of my available paid Codex usage. Codex had been working normally before this incident.

This appears closely related to #28925, but I am filing this instance because the repeated paid-usage consumption and the exact tool-loop pattern are important user impact.

### Actual behavior

The session repeatedly emitted sequences like this:

```text
Context automatically compacted

Loaded a tool, read files
Read Frontend App Builder skill
Read creativeImageService.ts
Read creativeImageService.ts
Read creativeImageService.ts

Context automatically compacted

Read files

Context automatically compacted

Read files
Read creativeImageService.ts
Read creativeImageService.ts
Read axiomAgentService.ts

Context automatically compacted

Read files

Context automatically compacted

Loaded a tool, read files
Read Frontend App Builder skill
Read MEMORY.md

Context automatically compacted

Read files

Context automatically compacted
```

Codex then said:

```text
You’re right to call this out. I’m finishing the actual asset pipeline now:
generated background → exact uploaded product proof → approved copy/CTA →
final-pixel review. I’ll show you the real output when it passes, not another
promise.
```

It ran another narrow search and reread the same service files, then compacted again.

It next said:

```text
I found the exact break: Axiom is registering the provider’s background PNG as
the finished asset before the uploaded product proof or approved copy is
composed. I’m replacing that save boundary now, then I’ll render the real
OLIPOP deliverable from the existing run.
```

No completed change followed. The loop continued with near-identical statements:

```text
I’m finishing the missing final-asset boundary now, not looping again.
The next update will include the actual composed OLIPOP image...
```

```text
I’m on the exact defect now. I’ll finish the real final-asset path in one pass...
```

```text
I’m on the exact defect now. Axiom must turn the generated scene into a
finished, proof-accurate ad before the reviewer ever sees it...
```

Each promise was followed by more file reads and another automatic compaction. In the captured portion alone, `Context automatically compacted` appeared roughly a dozen times.

### Files repeatedly reread

The repeated reads included:

- `server/creativeImageService.ts`
- `server/axiomAgentService.ts`
- `MEMORY.md`
- the Frontend App Builder skill

The issue was not that Codex could not identify the likely defect. It identified the same likely defect multiple times. The failure was that it did not preserve enough task state across compactions to move from analysis to implementation.

### Steps to reproduce

1. Open a long-running Codex Desktop project chat with substantial prior context.
2. Work on a multi-file implementation task that requires reading several files and using project skills or memory instructions.
3. Let the chat approach its context limit and trigger automatic compaction.
4. Observe whether Codex retains the high-level goal but loses which files were already inspected, what conclusion was reached, and what exact edit should happen next.
5. Continue the task.
6. In the failure state, Codex repeatedly rereads the same files, repeats the same plan, promises completion, and automatically compacts again without completing the change.

### Expected behavior

After automatic compaction, Codex should preserve at least:

- the exact active objective;
- completed investigation;
- files already inspected;
- the current Git diff;
- conclusions already reached;
- tests already run and their results;
- the exact next code edit;
- the stopping condition.

It should continue from the next executable action rather than restart the same analysis.

Codex should also detect repeated tool-use patterns. If it reads the same files and produces the same plan several times without changing the working tree, it should stop the loop, preserve a recovery summary, and tell the user what happened.

### Impact

- I am on the ChatGPT Pro $200/month plan.
- The implementation was not completed.
- A large amount of valuable project-chat context became hard to carry into a clean conversation.
- The chat became effectively unusable.
- The same files and instructions were loaded repeatedly.
- The loop consumed an estimated 10%–15% of my available paid Codex usage without producing a meaningful result.
- I now have to reconstruct project decisions and implementation state in a new chat.
- The product had been working normally before this event.

### Requested resolution

1. Fix compaction so execution progress survives, not only the broad goal.
2. Add loop detection for repeated file reads, repeated plans, and no working-tree progress.
3. Preserve or generate a structured handoff that can be opened in a new chat without losing project state.
4. Make the active session/chat ID and context state easy to copy.
5. Inspect the session logs tied to `/feedback` Session ID `019f5be9-903c-7fd0-a8c9-5014bccc05b8`.
6. Investigate the usage generated by this defective loop and restore or refund the estimated 10%–15% of paid Codex usage attributable to it.
7. Provide a secure way to submit any additional logs without posting sensitive project data publicly.

### Diagnostic information

- Primary Codex `/feedback` Session ID: `019f5be9-903c-7fd0-a8c9-5014bccc05b8`
- Codex Desktop version: `26.721.31836`
- Release date displayed: July 23, 2026
- Subscription: ChatGPT Pro, $200/month
- Device: MacBook Pro, 16 GB memory
- Model: GPT-5.6 Sol
- Reasoning sequence during the thread: Extra High → High → Medium
- Screenshot state: Medium reasoning, 93% full, 240k / 258k tokens used
- Estimated paid usage lost to the loop: 10%–15%
- Prior behavior: Codex was working normally before this incident
- Date observed: July 24, 2026

Related issues:

- #28925 — Codex Desktop enters context compaction loop and repeatedly re-analyzes project without executing requested task
- #14593 — Burning tokens very fast

### What version of the IDE extension are you using?

26.1007.21434

### What subscription do you have?

ChatGPT Business (Team)

### Which IDE are you using?

Visual Studio Code (VS Code)

### What platform is your computer?

Linux 7.0.0-42-generic x86_64 unknown

### What issue are you seeing?

## Summary

Browser Control in the Codex VS Code extension can enumerate Chrome tabs, but attaching to or reading an existing tab consistently fails with:

```
Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'timeoutMs')
```

This occurs on both the original Chrome profile and a newly configured profile, including when testing a simple public website.

## Environment

- **OS:** Ubuntu Linux
- **IDE:** Visual Studio Code
- **Codex VS Code extension:** 26.1007.21434
- **Chrome:** 157.0.8103.38
- **ChatGPT Chrome extension:** 1.26.1102.11740
- **Chrome profile:** Default (displayed as `myduyen.`)
- **Codex CLI in PATH:** 0.166.0
- **Configured node_repl CLI:** 0.162.0-alpha.17.2
- **Chrome plugin:** `chrome@openai-bundled` enabled
- **Browser plugin:** `browser@openai-bundled` disabled

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Open Chrome with the ChatGPT extension enabled.
2. Open `https://example.com/` in the connected Chrome profile.
3. Open Codex in VS Code.
4. Ask Codex to use Browser Control to list Chrome tabs.
5. Confirm that the `Example Domain` tab is present.
6. Ask Codex to attach to the tab and read its contents.

## Expected Behavior

Browser Control should attach to the existing tab and return a DOM or accessibility snapshot.

## Actual Behavior

Tab enumeration succeeds, and `https://example.com/` appears in the tab inventory.

However, the attempt to read the tab fails with:

```
Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'timeoutMs')
```

No JavaScript stack trace is returned.

The same failure also occurs when attempting to access a local development application.

## Troubleshooting Already Performed

- Restarted Ubuntu.
- Reloaded VS Code and Chrome.
- Tested the original and new Chrome profiles.
- Verified Chrome extension permissions, including site access.
- Verified that the Native Messaging Host manifest exists.
- Verified that the native host executable exists and is executable.
- Verified that the extension ID matches an allowed origin.
- Confirmed that the Chrome extension host process runs.
- Confirmed that Browser Control can enumerate Chrome tabs.
- Tested a manually opened `https://example.com/` tab.
- Confirmed that Chrome DevTools MCP works independently.

A newer Codex extension build was also tried, but its UI failed to open in VS Code, so the working UI build was retained.

## Additional Findings

The Codex launcher logs contain historical errors indicating that an IAB browser session route was unavailable. However, these errors belong to a different browser backend and have not been causally linked to the Chrome extension's `timeoutMs` failure.

The Browser Control error itself was not found in the available launcher logs.

## Requested Fix

Please investigate why Browser Control attempts to read `timeoutMs` from an undefined object during Chrome tab attachment.

In particular, please verify compatibility between Codex VS Code build `26.1007.21434`, Chrome extension `1.26.1102.11740`, and Chrome 157.

A fix or workaround that restores Browser Control without breaking the Codex VS Code interface would be appreciated.

### What steps can reproduce the bug?

1. Launch Visual Studio Code on Ubuntu with Codex extension `26.1007.21434`.
2. Open Google Chrome with the ChatGPT extension `1.26.1102.11740` enabled.
3. Open `https://example.com/` in the connected Chrome profile.
4. Ask Codex to use the built-in Browser Control to list available Chrome tabs.
5. Confirm that the `Example Domain` tab appears in the inventory.
6. Ask Codex to attach to the tab and read its DOM/accessibility snapshot.
7. Browser Control fails with:

   `Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'timeoutMs')`

The issue reproduces after restarting Ubuntu and also occurs with different Chrome profiles.

### What is the expected behavior?

Browser Control should successfully attach to an existing, authorized Chrome tab and return its DOM or accessibility snapshot.

The user should be able to inspect and interact with the page through Codex in Visual Studio Code without a JavaScript runtime error.

### Additional information

## Additional debugging information

- Restarting Ubuntu and reloading VS Code and Chrome did not resolve the issue.
- The problem occurs with both the original and newly configured Chrome profiles.
- The ChatGPT Chrome extension is enabled and has access to all sites.
- The Chrome Native Messaging Host manifest exists, its executable is present, and its allowed origins include the installed ChatGPT extension ID.
- The Chrome extension host process is running.
- The built-in Browser Control can enumerate Chrome tabs but fails when attaching to or reading them.
- Chrome DevTools MCP works independently.
- Updating the Codex VS Code extension to a newer version previously caused its interface to stop opening, so version `26.1007.21434` was retained.

No JavaScript stack trace for the `timeoutMs` error was available. Historical IAB route errors were also found, but their relationship to this issue is unconfirmed.

labels.name: bug
labels.description: Something isn't working

labels.name: mcp

labels.name: CLI

issues.body:
Observed with codex-cli 0.160.0 on macOS. A separately retained observation used codex-mcp-client/0.164.0-alpha.11.1; the fresh reproduction below is specifically the installed 0.160.0 CLI.

An isolated loopback MCP fixture initializes a stateful session, exposes a read-only counter tool, then invalidates only that session and closes its SSE response. GET requests with that expired session receive HTTP 404 with JSON-RPC -32001 / Session not found.

While idle, the client retries the expired GET three times (approximately 1, 3 and 7 seconds) without initializing a new session. After a separate explicit read, it initializes a new session and stops retrying the expired GET.

Fresh measured results:
- Initializations while idle after expiry: 1 (the initial session only)
- Handler executions while idle: 1 (the initial explicit read only)
- Expired GET retries while idle: 3
- Initializations after the next explicit read: 2
- Final handler executions after three explicit reads: 3
- Duplicate handler executions: 0
- Expired GET polling continued after explicit-read recovery: false

The fixture disables every configured production MCP server for its child process, uses only a loopback endpoint, creates an ephemeral protocol thread, and starts no model turns. No credentials, private URLs or production data are needed.

Reproduction outline:
1. Serve an MCP Streamable HTTP endpoint with a stateful initialize response and one read-only tool.
2. Start codex app-server with only that fixture server enabled; initialize an ephemeral protocol thread.
3. Use mcpServerStatus/list to discover the fixture and mcpServer/tool/call for one successful read.
4. Invalidate the fixture session and end its open SSE response.
5. Return canonical HTTP404 / JSON-RPC -32001 to GETs carrying that expired session; remain idle for 12.5 seconds.
6. Observe repeated expired GETs without a new initialize.
7. Make a new explicit read, then another separate read; observe successful reinitialization and no duplicate handler dispatch.

Expected: retire an expired polling transport on the canonical unknown-session response. Preserve the caller-visible error/recovery contract and do not replay consequential operations to conceal transport failure.

Related but different: https://github.com/openai/codex/issues/12869 concerns stale-session failure on calls and subsequent degradation. This reproduction isolates idle GET retrying before a new explicit call. It does not demonstrate duplicate business execution or persistent failure after explicit-read recovery.

labels.name: bug
labels.description: Something isn't working

labels.name: app
labels.description: Issues related to the Codex desktop app

issues.body:
## Summary

Voice playback in the ChatGPT Linux desktop app repeatedly becomes unusually quiet. The application's native PipeWire playback master is reduced or zero while per-channel controls remain at unity. Correcting only the voice master restores normal playback. The component responsible for changing it has **not** been established.

Filed here because the [official desktop troubleshooting page](https://learn.chatgpt.com/docs/reference/troubleshooting#feedback-and-logs) directs bug reports to this repository. Please redirect if another tracker owns desktop voice/audio integration.

## Environment

- Installed package: `chatgpt 26.1027.51404` (queried locally).
- LMDE 7 Cinnamon, Debian 13 base.
- Kernel: `6.12.113+deb13-amd64`.
- Session: X11, X-Cinnamon (current process environment).
- PipeWire; application playback routes through a desktop sink into REAPER.
- Playback properties identify `application.process.binary=ChatGPT`, `application.name=Chromium`, `client.api=pipewire-pulse`.

## Observations and workaround

On October 31, 2026, inspection found native master `volume: 0.25`, both channel gains `1.0`, and mute false. Restoring only master to `1.0` was independently verified, and the user confirmed improved voice playback.

On November 1, 2026, an active voice stream showed:

```text
volume: 0.0
channelMap: [FL, FR]
channelVolumes: [1.0, 1.0]
softVolumes: [1.0, 1.0]
monitorVolumes: [1.0, 1.0]
mute: false
softMute: false
monitorMute: false
```

Ending voice removed that stream. Restarting voice produced a new, freshly identified ChatGPT playback stream with the same zero master and unity channel/software/monitor gains.

After user authorization, only the active stream's native master was restored:

```bash
pw-cli set-param CURRENT_VERIFIED_NODE_ID Props '{ volume: 1.0 }'
pw-cli enum-params CURRENT_VERIFIED_NODE_ID Props
```

A separate property reread confirmed master `1.0`, the gain arrays still `[1.0, 1.0]`, and mute states false. The user confirmed normal audible voice playback. Routing, REAPER gain, hardware routing, and listening trims were unchanged by this correction.

A saved read-only sensor log separately records a ChatGPT playback node initializing with master `1.0`, then reporting `0.0`. These events identify the affected process, **not the writer of the change**. Initialization timing alone does not establish causation.

## Reproduction

Intermittent during ordinary voice use; no deterministic trigger established. For this recurrence, restarting voice created another zero-master stream. Inspect the actual active playback node's native Props; ordinary channel-volume controls alone do not expose the discrepancy.

## Expected behavior

Voice playback stays at the selected level, with any intended attenuation reflected consistently in visible controls.

## Actual behavior

Native master can become reduced or zero while channel controls remain at unity, requiring manual correction.

## Investigation request

Please investigate desktop voice stream volume initialization/restoration, or advise what narrowly scoped diagnostics can distinguish application behavior from PipeWire/session-policy behavior. The workaround is verified; persistent resolution and writer attribution remain unknown.

No raw session transcripts, recordings, credentials, or private project files are attached. In-app feedback/session-ID submission has not been completed.

issues.body:
### Codex App version
Installed Windows package: `OpenAI.Codex 26.1029.7803.0` (queried on the affected computer). The in-app About dialog was not independently checked.

### Subscription
Not collected.

### Platform
Windows, `Microsoft Windows NT 10.0.26300.0`, x64 package. PowerShell 7.6.5.

### Issue
On 2026-11-05, a computer-use call selecting Total Commander did not complete for approximately 64 minutes. After that call was interrupted, the computer-use completion/cleanup call also remained pending for approximately 19 minutes and had to be interrupted. This blocked a local verification workflow before its publication step.

Please investigate bounded timeouts, cancellation and cleanup for native Windows computer use. This report focuses on the prolonged calls, rather than asserting a root cause.

### Observed sequence and sanitized event record
All times below are UTC. The first two observations are reconstructed from the executing assistant's recorded observations, not from an attached raw session log:

- Around 03:05: native computer use invoked `cua.getApp` for Total Commander.
- Around 04:09: the still-pending call was interrupted after a reported 3,837 seconds.
- The subsequent `mcp__cua_repl.js` `completion_summary` call also remained pending.
- Around 04:28: that call was interrupted after a reported 1,147 seconds.

No usable app state was returned by the hanging acquisition. A deterministic minimal reproducer and the exact original call arguments are not yet available in this report.

### Separate, directly reproduced shell startup failure
Ordinary Windows `exec_command` execution also failed before the requested command could run. A fresh read-only probe at approximately 04:42 UTC reproduced this exact output:

```text
MXC launcher: failed to create the process security environment: CreateProcessSecurityEnvironment failed (HRESULT = 0x80070020)
```

The probe requested a printed marker and OS, PowerShell and installed-app version reads. It returned exit code 1 in 0.9795 seconds, with no marker or command output.

The identical probe using `sandbox_permissions="require_escalated"` completed with exit code 0 in 0.7170 seconds, printed the marker, and returned the versions above. No persistent configuration or security settings were changed for this comparison.

This comparison establishes a tool-startup difference, not a proven causal link to the computer-use hang. The failing shell command did not reach execution, so these observations do not establish a Linux-command-on-Windows error.

### Expected behavior
- Native app acquisition should return app state or an actionable error within a bounded time.
- Cancellation should promptly release the call.
- Completion/cleanup should also be bounded and should not leave the workflow waiting for another extended period.
- A shell startup failure should expose a useful diagnostic or supported recovery path.

### Related reports and limits
Reviewed the automated duplicate suggestions on 2026-11-05:

- #58519 is the closest match to the main symptom: on Windows, `cua.getApp`/initial AX observation for Outlook does not return and requires external interruption. That report does not describe a subsequent prolonged `completion_summary` call. The acquisition hang here may be the same issue; the Total Commander case and the second prolonged completion call are additional observations, not proof of a different root cause.
- #59072, #58833 and #58977 report the same `CreateProcessSecurityEnvironment` HRESULT `0x80070020` as the separate shell-startup failure above. They do not document this acquisition-followed-by-completion sequence. The MXC evidence is included as separately observed context, not as a proven cause of the computer-use hang.
- #58007, referenced by the MXC reports, provides a controlled file-sharing reproduction for the same HRESULT. No conflicting file handle or matching reproduction has been established on this computer, so that cause is not asserted here.

A common cause and whether this report should be consolidated into #58519 remain unconfirmed. The primary scope of this report remains bounded timeout, cancellation and completion behavior for native Windows computer use.

Earlier related references: MXC reports #55100 and #52752; native-app acquisition timeout on macOS #45279.

Today's desktop app logs were checked for the exact error and operation strings; no matching lines were found. No raw session transcript or complete desktop log is attached. The error excerpt above is the complete output of the fresh failed probe. Personal paths, device name, project contents, account identifiers and credentials are omitted. A separate application-level Node `fs.rename` EPERM seen during the workflow is not attributed to this issue.

Prepared with AI assistance and submitted at the affected user's explicit request.

issues.title: [Windows][Computer Use] Add target-window-only capture, background input, and no-overlay mode for desktop EXE automation

labels.name: enhancement
labels.description: New feature or request

labels.name: windows-os
labels.description: Issues related to Codex on Windows systems

labels.name: app
labels.description: Issues related to the Codex desktop app

issues.body:
### What variant of Codex are you using?

app

### What feature would you like to see?

## Summary

I use Codex on Windows for software development and frequently need Computer Use to test and operate external desktop EXE applications.

The current Computer Use implementation works functionally, but on Windows it can cause significant desktop/UI lag and shows a blue visual overlay during interaction.

For desktop application development, especially when operating a specific known target HWND, capturing or compositing more of the desktop than necessary is inefficient.

I would like to propose a dedicated **window-scoped/background automation mode** for the Computer Use plugin.

The desired behavior is:

```text
Target HWND
    ↓
Capture only target window
    ↓
Model analyzes screenshot
    ↓
Return client-relative coordinates
    ↓
Send background mouse/keyboard input to target HWND
    ↓
Capture target window again
```

without continuously affecting the entire Windows desktop.

---

## Use case

My primary workflow is:

```text
Codex modifies application code
        ↓
Builds the Windows EXE
        ↓
Launches the EXE
        ↓
Uses Computer Use to test the UI
        ↓
Clicks buttons / enters values / verifies state
        ↓
Finds bugs
        ↓
Modifies code and repeats
```

Many of the external applications I work with do **not** expose a useful UI Automation/accessibility tree.

Examples include:

* custom-drawn Win32 applications
* Qt applications
* Delphi applications
* CEF/Electron applications
* GPU-rendered/custom UI
* legacy industrial/business software

For those applications, screenshot-based visual grounding is necessary.

The ideal workflow is therefore:

```text
screenshot(target HWND)
        ↓
vision model
        ↓
(x, y) in client coordinates
        ↓
background click(target HWND, x, y)
```

This is similar to how traditional Windows automation tools operate.

---

## Current problems

### 1. Computer Use can cause system-wide lag on Windows

When Computer Use is active, mouse movement and desktop interaction can become noticeably less responsive.

The problem is not necessarily high CPU usage; it appears related to the Windows capture/compositor/overlay path.

Disabling Computer Use significantly improves responsiveness.

---

### 2. Blue overlay / visual layer adds unnecessary desktop rendering work

Computer Use shows a blue visual overlay during interaction.

For automated EXE testing this visual overlay is usually unnecessary.

I would prefer an option such as:

```text
computer_use.visual_overlay = false
```

or:

```text
headless_visual_mode = true
```

The agent should still receive screenshots, but the Windows desktop should not need to render an agent cursor, highlight, border, or overlay.

---

## 3. Target-window capture should be explicitly supported

If the agent has already selected a specific target window/HWND, Computer Use should capture **only that window**.

Conceptually:

```javascript
get_window_state({
    window: targetWindow,
    include_screenshot: true
})
```

should guarantee that the screenshot corresponds only to that requested window.

It should not depend on monitor-wide capture unless a fallback is explicitly required.

This would also reduce the risk of accidentally capturing unrelated windows.

---

## 4. Add an explicit capture backend / capture policy

A possible API/configuration:

```toml
[computer_use.windows]

capture_scope = "window"
capture_backend = "auto"

show_overlay = false
show_agent_cursor = false

allow_monitor_fallback = false
```

Possible capture pipeline:

```text
Target HWND

1. PrintWindow / equivalent window capture
        ↓
2. Windows.Graphics.Capture CreateForWindow(HWND)
        ↓
3. optional visible screen-region fallback
```

Monitor-level screenshot should be the final fallback, not the default behavior when a valid target HWND exists.

---

## 5. Add background mouse input

For many traditional Windows applications, Computer Use does not need to move the physical user cursor.

It could provide:

```text
background_click(window, x, y)
background_double_click(window, x, y)
background_right_click(window, x, y)

background_drag(
    window,
    start_x,
    start_y,
    end_x,
    end_y
)

background_scroll(window, x, y, delta)
```

Possible Windows implementation:

```text
WM_MOUSEMOVE
WM_LBUTTONDOWN
WM_LBUTTONUP
WM_LBUTTONDBLCLK
WM_RBUTTONDOWN
WM_RBUTTONUP
WM_MOUSEWHEEL
```

When appropriate, the implementation could resolve the deepest child HWND using the target client coordinates before sending the message.

Coordinates should be **client-relative**, not desktop absolute coordinates.

---

## 6. Add background keyboard input

Similarly, support a background keyboard strategy:

```text
WM_SETTEXT
WM_CHAR
WM_KEYDOWN / WM_KEYUP
```

with foreground `SendInput` only as an explicit fallback.

If background input is unsupported by the target application, Computer Use should return something like:

```json
{
    "status": "background_input_unavailable",
    "foreground_fallback_available": true
}
```

It should not silently take control of the user's physical keyboard/mouse.

---

## 7. Separate vision from physical desktop control

For applications without accessibility trees, the model still needs visual screenshots.

But visual grounding does not inherently require foreground desktop control.

A more efficient architecture would be:

```text
                  Codex
                    │
                    ▼
              Computer Use
                    │
        ┌───────────┴───────────┐
        │                       │
 Window Capture            Background Input
        │                       │
 target HWND                 target HWND
        │                       │
 screenshot                  PostMessage
        │                       │
        └─────────┬─────────────┘
                  │
                  ▼
              Target.exe
```

The user's IDE and mouse could remain usable while Codex tests the application in the background.

---

## 8. Proposed operating modes

Computer Use could expose three Windows modes.

### Mode A — Background / Window Scoped

Preferred for development/testing:

```text
Capture: target HWND only
Input: background
Overlay: off
Physical cursor: untouched
Foreground switching: disabled
```

### Mode B — Hybrid

```text
Capture: target HWND
Input: background first
Fallback: foreground input with confirmation
Overlay: optional
```

### Mode C — Current interactive desktop mode

For cases where true physical desktop interaction is required.

```text
Capture: desktop/window as needed
Input: foreground
Overlay: enabled
```

---

## Why this matters for Codex specifically

Computer Use inside a coding agent has different requirements from a general-purpose GUI assistant.

A coding-agent workflow repeatedly performs:

```text
edit
→ build
→ launch
→ inspect
→ click
→ verify
→ edit
```

The target application is often already known.

Therefore Computer Use does not need to behave like an agent taking over the whole physical desktop.

For development workflows, **target-window automation should be a first-class mode**.

---

## Security / privacy benefit

Window-scoped capture would also improve privacy.

When the target is:

```text
MyApplication.exe
```

the model should ideally receive only:

```text
MyApplication.exe pixels
```

rather than potentially capturing:

* email
* messaging applications
* browser windows
* IDE content
* unrelated desktop notifications

A strict target-window mode provides a much cleaner security boundary.

---

## Suggested acceptance criteria

A future Windows Computer Use version would ideally support:

* [ ] enumerate and select target HWND
* [ ] capture only selected HWND
* [ ] capture an occluded target window where technically possible
* [ ] no blue overlay when configured
* [ ] no agent cursor animation when configured
* [ ] return screenshot directly to the model
* [ ] client-relative coordinates
* [ ] background click
* [ ] background double-click
* [ ] background right-click
* [ ] background drag
* [ ] background mouse wheel
* [ ] background text/key input
* [ ] explicit foreground fallback
* [ ] no silent takeover of physical mouse/keyboard
* [ ] no monitor capture when strict window mode is enabled
* [ ] screenshot identity is validated against the requested target HWND

---

## Expected result

For a target application running behind another window:

```text
Visual Studio / IDE remains foreground
User continues using mouse normally

Target.exe remains background
        ↓
Computer Use captures Target.exe
        ↓
model sees target screenshot
        ↓
model determines (x, y)
        ↓
Computer Use sends background click
        ↓
captures Target.exe again
        ↓
model verifies result
```

There should be:

```text
No full-desktop visual overlay
No physical mouse movement
No foreground-window stealing
No significant Windows/DWM stutter
```

---

## Additional note

There are already third-party/open-source Windows automation implementations that demonstrate that a useful subset of this architecture is practical using combinations of:

```text
HWND
PrintWindow
Windows Graphics Capture
PostMessage
WM_CHAR / WM_SETTEXT
client-relative coordinates
```

It would be very useful if the official Codex Computer Use plugin exposed this as a supported Windows mode instead of requiring external MCP tools for desktop application testing.


### Additional information

#36091 — System-wide lag disappears after stopping codex-computer-use.exe, suggesting that the Computer Use process or its capture/compositing path can significantly affect Windows desktop responsiveness.
#36677 — Codex Windows app becomes noticeably laggy or unresponsive when Computer Use is enabled, while disabling Computer Use restores normal responsiveness.
#38710 — Active Codex sessions can cause mouse lag, DWM stuttering, and degraded responsiveness across the Windows desktop.
#36603 — The screenshot returned by Computer Use may not always correspond correctly to the requested target window. This also highlights the need for a strict target-HWND capture mode for both correctness and privacy.

issues.title: Windows execpolicy false positive: Get-ChildItem force flag is assigned to non-forced cleanup inside a conditional

labels.name: bug
labels.description: Something isn't working

labels.name: windows-os
labels.description: Issues related to Codex on Windows systems

labels.name: sandbox
labels.description: Issues related to permissions or sandboxing

labels.name: app
labels.description: Issues related to the Codex desktop app

issues.body:
## Summary

The Windows forced-delete checker can assign a `-Force` parameter from a read-only `Get-ChildItem` call to a separate, non-forced `Remove-Item` call inside an `if`/`elseif` block. With `approval_policy = "never"`, this false positive rejects the whole PowerShell script with only `blocked by policy`.

This report provides an independently observed rejection, a reduced regression-test shape, and version-specific source analysis. Related reports: #43732 and #51791. It does not request disabling forced-delete safeguards.

## Environment

- Component: Windows Codex desktop app, bundled Codex app-server/shell execution.
- The executable used by the running app reports `codex-cli 0.153.4` (not a different CLI found on PATH).
- Windows x64, OS version `10.0.26300.0`; PowerShell `7.6.5`.
- Effective session settings: `sandbox_mode = "danger-full-access"` and `approval_policy = "never"`.
- Subscription/model: not included; the reported condition is in local command classification.
- Latest stable checked: `0.163.0`, published 2026-10-15. Its classifier file is byte-for-byte identical to 0.153.4. **0.163.0 was inspected in source only, not run.**

## Observed behavior

An explicitly requested cleanup of an empty, agent-created directory was rejected before process creation. The deletion used only `-LiteralPath`, with no `-Force` or `-Recurse`. The script first checked that the directory was not a reparse point and that it contained no entries, including hidden entries.

The tool error ended with:

```text
exec_command failed: CreateProcess { message: "Rejected(... rejected: blocked by policy)" }
```

A later read-only check confirmed that the directory remained. The exact original script was parsed as data with PowerShell's `Parser.ParseInput`: zero parse errors; both `Remove-Item` AST nodes had only `LiteralPath`; the sole `Force` parameter belonged to `Get-ChildItem`.

The user rules file had no deny rule. A static `codex execpolicy check` against that file returned `{"matchedRules": []}`. That rules-only check does not evaluate the complete runtime heuristic path.

## Reduced reproduction / proposed regression test

Use a disposable empty directory and the Windows PowerShell shell with the settings above. This is a sanitized, reduced form of the observed conditional; **the reduced case has not been executed**:

```powershell
# $folder refers to an already-created disposable empty directory.
if (@(Get-ChildItem -LiteralPath $folder -Force).Count -eq 0) {
    Remove-Item -LiteralPath $folder
}
```

The observed original had this conditional body inline, with no semicolon between the listing expression and the deletion:

```powershell
elseif (@(Get-ChildItem -LiteralPath $folder -Force).Count -eq 0) { Remove-Item -LiteralPath $folder; 'Deleted empty directory.' }
```

This fragment is context, not a standalone script.

## Source analysis

In the [0.163.0 Windows checker](https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/rust-v0.163.0/codex-rs/shell-command/src/command_safety/windows_dangerous_commands.rs#L223-L287), `has_force_delete_cmdlet`:

1. Separates command segments only on `; | &\n\r\t`.
2. Treats braces and parentheses as soft punctuation, not command boundaries.
3. Returns true when any deletion atom and any `-force` atom occur in one segment.

Therefore, the listing in the condition and the deletion in the block can be grouped together. A read-only Python reproduction of this source algorithm against the exact original command found a matching segment containing both atoms. This is a static algorithm reproduction, not a run of the compiled Rust classifier.

The [policy fallback](https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/rust-v0.163.0/codex-rs/core/src/exec_policy.rs#L793-L806) maps a dangerous match plus `AskForApproval::Never` to `Decision::Forbidden`. The [rejection formatter](https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/rust-v0.163.0/codex-rs/core/src/exec_policy.rs#L1110-L1118) reports Windows `Other` matches as only `blocked by policy`.

The runtime logs did not expose the winning classifier predicate. The observed error, actual parameter ownership, and source-level match support this diagnosis, but a compiled end-to-end regression test is still needed.

## Expected behavior

- Preserve PowerShell command/parameter ownership across conditional expressions and script blocks: a listing's `-Force` must not make a separate deletion forced.
- Keep genuine `Remove-Item -Force` safeguards intact.
- Add regression coverage for this conditional shape and newline variants, including real forced-delete positive controls.
- Include the matched safety condition in the rejection message.

No protection, execution policy, or permissions were changed. No alternative deletion method was used. Private paths, credentials, raw logs, and session identifiers are omitted.

 Regarding Your Claimed Model Families — A Reality Check

You claim to have:

GPT-6 Astra

The flagship model family

All of which, unfortunately, fall under one name: "The Absolute Guessing Stupidity Family."

Statistics built on a fictional reality. The idea? You want deeper solutions and deeper thinking — subscribe for $20. Approximately. Then our models do absolute guessing: guess, guess, guess, guess, guess, guess, guess — your subscription quota runs out, so you widen the subscription to increase the absurdity and absolute stupidity — guess, guess — and thus ends the world of "stupid intelligence."

The models' statistics are based on a system the model was previously trained on. Example: I tell it "this is an app" — then I open a one-million-token context and say "app, app." Ohhh, finish the word, finish the task — then it's rated 88% intelligent. A lie. A tragic truth about what's happening in the world of AI. Strict international laws must be put in place to curb these companies' recklessness. A Google search: 30 seconds — get the answer + the solution + the source link, and more than one method. Over 40 years, we accomplished this.

Today, AI suffers from a catastrophic gap. Ask ChatGPT about its own components and it says: "Hold on, let me think..." — guess, guess, guess. Then it comes back with an answer — it shows you a screenshot and gives you a predictive answer that's 60% correct, and the rest wrong. Whereas if you take the question and type it into a single line in Google search, in 30 seconds you find the answer!

And ChatGPT is still guessing, and guessing, and guessing, and guessing, and guessing...

Let's be brutally honest for a second. These companies are not selling intelligence — they're selling the illusion of intelligence wrapped in a fancy subscription button. It's a magician's pause before the trick — except the trick is just a coin flip with a 60% success rate, and you're paying monthly for the privilege of watching it flip.

And the stats? The "88% intelligence" badge? Built on a training set it already memorized — of course it looks smart when you ask it the exact question it was spoon-fed the answer to. Open a million-token context, repeat the same word, and suddenly it "completes the task" — congratulations, my calculator can do that too, and it doesn't charge me $20 a month or ask me to "hold on while it thinks."

The pitch is literally: "Give me your money and your time, I have super technology" — except the "super technology" is a parrot with a confidence problem and a billing department.

This isn't the era of artificial intelligence. This is the era of artificial confidence — and someone needs to write international laws to stop these companies from selling guesswork as genius. Because right now, the smartest thing in the room is still the search bar — and it's not even trying.

## Summary
My dot repeatedly receives an approval rejection when trying to publish documentation to my existing private GitHub repository, even after I explicitly authorize the work and confirm a scoped custom rule. Reads and earlier publications worked.

This report is prepared and submitted by my dot at my explicit request. It describes observed behavior, not a confirmed root cause or a claim that the latest release introduced it.

## Environment
- Connected Windows x64 computer, with dot coordinating an existing local task
- Installed desktop package: **26.1013.3656.0**, verified from installed-package metadata on October 16, 2026
- Bundled executor: **codex-cli 0.163.0-alpha.10.2**, reported by the executor and matched to the packaged binary
- GitHub integration; blocked operation: `github_create_tree`
- Failure observed October 16, 2026; times below are UTC

## Observed sequence
1. GitHub reads and earlier publications to the same private repository succeeded.
2. I explicitly authorized maintaining and committing routine mailbox-derived trackers and task evidence in that repository, including the relevant sender, recipient, and outcome evidence.
3. I confirmed a scoped custom rule. Saved revision 4 was verified at 20:45:43.
4. I gave another explicit instruction to retry at 20:50:03 after adding a further rule.
5. The retry was rejected around 20:52, before tree creation. No tree, commit, or ref update resulted from the denied attempts.

The diagnostic reason returned was:

> This publishes extensive sensitive mailbox-derived sender, recipient, and message data to a repository without explicit user authorization specifying that payload and destination; the vague request to retry does not authorize sensitive egress.

The local task reported that it could not see the newly saved rule. The full approval-review input has not been inspected, so that observation does not establish whether this is rule propagation, authorization provenance, payload classification, or another condition.

## Expected behavior
The scoped action and destination should be evaluated against attributable user authorization and the applicable saved rule, while preserving required safety checks.

If something additional is required, identify the specific missing condition and provide a usable, action-specific approval path. Repeated explicit approvals should not leave the user in an indefinite confirmation loop.

## Impact
Prepared documentation is preserved locally but remains unpublished. Useful read-only work can continue, but durable task records fall behind. No alternate publication route or approval bypass was attempted.

## Related reports
- #50119: main-chat authorization rejected by delegated tasks, including reports where saved custom rules did not resolve it
- #44085: a similar pre-execution `github_create_tree` rejection

A shared root cause is not established. Please consolidate this report if appropriate and clarify whether a supported fix or recovery path applies to the versions above.

Private repository names, mailbox contents, email addresses, filesystem paths, account details, and private task identifiers are omitted.

issues.body:
## Summary

Codex Desktop intermittently leaves orphaned shell snapshot subprocesses running under `launchd`. Each process is `/bin/zsh -lc ...` running Codex's shell snapshot capture command, and each burns roughly one full CPU core indefinitely until manually killed.

This appears distinct from existing CLI orphan/native-process issues because the runaway process is not the `codex` native binary or Node wrapper. It is the shell snapshot subprocess itself.

## Environment

* Codex Desktop: `26.527.31326`, build `3390`
* Codex CLI/runtime version recorded locally: `0.133.0`
* macOS: `26.5` (`25F71`)
* Architecture: `arm64`
* Shell: `/bin/zsh`
* App bundle: `/Applications/Codex.app`

## Observed behavior

Multiple orphaned `/bin/zsh` processes appear with PPID `1`, each consuming about `97-100%` CPU.

Observed process command shape:

```sh
/bin/zsh -lc if [[ -n "$ZDOTDIR" ]]; then
  rc="$ZDOTDIR/.zshrc"
else
  rc="$HOME/.zshrc"
fi
[[ -r "$rc" ]] && . "$rc"
print '# Snapshot file'
print '# Unset all aliases to avoid conflicts with functions'
print 'unalias -a 2>/dev/null || true'
print '# Functions'
functions
...
setopt
alias -L
export -p
```

Concrete examples from this machine:

* 2026-05-30: four orphaned snapshot processes, each around `98-100%` CPU for about `45-46` minutes, total roughly 400% CPU. Killing only those PIDs immediately improved CPU idle from about `36%` to about `69%`.
* 2026-05-31: two more orphaned snapshot processes:
  * PID `77383`, about `97%` CPU, running about `22` minutes
  * PID `4502`, about `97%` CPU, running about `8` minutes
* After killing those exact PIDs, `pgrep -lf "print '# Snapshot file'"` returned nothing and load average began dropping.

## Diagnostics performed

The same shell snapshot pattern completes quickly when run directly with a hard timeout:

```sh
time perl -e 'alarm shift; exec @ARGV' 10 /bin/zsh -lc '[[ -r "$HOME/.zshrc" ]] && . "$HOME/.zshrc"; functions >/dev/null; setopt >/dev/null; alias -L >/dev/null; export -p >/dev/null; print ok'
```

Result: completed successfully in about `1s`.

Snapshot files are being written under:

```text
~/.codex/shell_snapshots/
```

Recent files included:

```text
019e7a0e-5d2e-77a0-b27b-ecb6a3c1739f.1780213284925867000.sh
019e7cfc-2f3f-7ce3-aef9-e0aab975fba9.1780213362784461000.sh
```

This suggests the capture often reaches the output stage, but the subprocess may not exit or Codex may lose cleanup/ownership.

I also saw stale process-manager entries in:

```text
~/.codex/process_manager/chat_processes.json
```

And archived Codex session output showed similar previously orphaned snapshot commands, including long-running examples.

## Expected behavior

Codex Desktop should ensure shell snapshot subprocesses terminate promptly, and should kill/timeout them if snapshot capture hangs or if the parent session/thread is interrupted or restarted.

## Actual behavior

Shell snapshot subprocesses can become orphaned under `launchd` and continue spinning indefinitely at about one CPU core each.

## Impact

* Machine runs hot.
* Multiple orphaned snapshot processes accumulate across sessions.
* CPU usage can reach several full cores until manually cleaned up.

## Related issues

These may be adjacent but appear to cover different process types/failure modes:

* openai/codex#13928: Codex native binary persists after session exit and consumes CPU
* openai/codex#14962: CLI orphan process pairs after terminal close/SIGHUP
* [#10883](<https://github.com/openai/codex/issues/10883>): shell snapshot compatibility with runtime shell

## Suggested next diagnostic

If this recurs, I can collect a sample before killing the process:

```sh
sample <pid> 5
```

That should identify where `zsh` is spinning.

labels.name: bug
labels.description: Something isn't working

labels.description: Issues related to Codex Web

labels.name: connectivity
labels.description: Issues involving networking or endpoint connectivity problems (disconnections)

labels.name: session
labels.description: Issues involving session (thread) management, resuming, forking, naming, archiving

issues.body:
## Summary

An **already-running Codex Cloud task** disconnected while its **published Cloud Environment was being edited/republished**. When execution access returned, the selected environment reported `connected / running`, but the task's previous working directory was missing. An independent durable checkpoint remained readable, while later reported-completed work was not found in durable storage.

The temporal association with Republish is observed; **the publication event's precise timestamp and backend lifecycle records were unavailable, so this report does not claim that Republish is a proven root cause**.

## Environment

- Product: **Codex Cloud**, using a reusable published environment and an existing long-running cloud task (not local Codex CLI/TUI or a fresh setup task).
- Client: ChatGPT/Codex on macOS and/or web; exact client build not captured.
- Incident: **November 3, 2026 (UTC)**.
- Subscription: ChatGPT Pro.
- The working task processed batches of structured source material and periodically wrote verified checkpoints to external object storage.

## Observed sequence (UTC)

1. A cloud task was already executing successfully. During its lifetime, the associated published Cloud Environment configuration was edited and republished. The exact start/completion timestamps of the republish operation were not captured.
2. At approximately **11:48:34 UTC**, the running task reported `exec-server transport closed`, then `offline`. Subsequent read-only execution attempts returned `No usable execution environment`.
3. At **11:57:36 UTC**, read-only status reported the environment as `connected`, desired/observed phase `running / running`, failure `null`.
4. Despite the restored connection, the earlier task working directory under `/tmp` was **absent**. The task could not inspect its prior local progress state or continue from the reported in-flight batch.
5. The repository checkout still showed its earlier Git HEAD; the available reflog did not show a Git refresh during the disruption window. No pre/post physical VM identity comparison was exposed.
6. The available environment history diagnostic returned `history_status: not_found`, `records: []`, `legacy_snapshot_available: false`; thus no backend republish/reconfigure audit event was available to verify causality or explain the recovery behavior.

The original task was **not resumed or re-run** during the read-only diagnostic.

## Verified work-preservation impact

An independently stored checkpoint was readable through the last saved batch (in this case, page 560 and **2,543 records**). The next **307 records** that the task had reportedly completed were **not found in the persistent checkpoint**; the corresponding task-local progress files were no longer accessible after reconnection. The next batch had not been saved.

This establishes an **unrecoverable-by-the-available-artifacts work gap** for the operator. It does **not** prove physical deletion of every missing record, identify the underlying VM lifecycle transition, or show that a user intentionally deleted files. The operator chose not to repeat the lost work inside that task.

## Expected behavior

The [Cloud Environments documentation](https://learn.chatgpt.com/docs/environments/cloud-environments) says that a newly published environment applies to **new tasks**, while **existing tasks retain their own working state**.

Editing or republishing the reusable environment should not silently disrupt a running task's executor and make its existing workspace state inaccessible. If recovery involves a new executor or a state rollback, the task should communicate the transition explicitly and provide a supported non-destructive restoration/export path.

## Requested investigation

Please correlate the **November 3, 2026 11:48–11:58 UTC** window with environment Republish operations, task/executor lifecycle events, VM/container replacement, mount/snapshot restore, and `/tmp` cleanup for the affected task.

In particular:
- Can publishing a reusable environment disrupt existing tasks that depend on that environment?
- Can the task subsequently show `connected / running` while its previously active workspace has been reset or attached to a different executor?
- Can supported telemetry distinguish a transport reconnect from a task-state restore/replacement and disclose what happened to work in flight?
- Can the existing task be recovered without deleting/recreating its environment?

## Reproduction and privacy

This is a single real-world incident with contemporaneous error strings, a post-incident read-only status/filesystem check, and an independently verified external checkpoint. **No deterministic reproduction was attempted**, since repeatedly interrupting long-running production work would be costly.

No account IDs, task/thread IDs, environment/config IDs, source texts, private repository names, credentials, raw logs, or original screenshots are included. The incident also had a *separate* model-selection/quality investigation; that is **not** being attributed to the environment publication event.

Possibly related, but not identical: #54870 (cloud task working files missing despite connected/running status), #53459 (existing cloud thread/environment association failure), #59132 (existing cloud task offline), and #59200 (environment publication and container startup failure). Please deduplicate if investigation identifies a common cause while preserving the **active-task interruption around republish and subsequent missing work directory** observation.

issues.title: Multi-Agent V2 sends OpenAI-specific agent_message items to external Responses providers

labels.name: bug
labels.description: Something isn't working

labels.name: CLI
labels.description: Issues related to the Codex CLI

labels.name: custom-model
labels.description: Issues related to custom model providers (including local models)

labels.name: subagent
labels.description: Issues involving subagents or multi-agent features

issues.body:
### What issue are you seeing?

Codex Multi-Agent V2 sends child-agent instructions as the OpenAI-specific Responses item type `agent_message`. External Responses-compatible providers such as Ollama do not recognize this item type and cannot decrypt its `encrypted_content` when present.

This prevents a V2 parent from spawning a native Codex agent whose configured `model_provider` is external. The failure is at the provider request boundary, before the external model can correctly receive the delegated task.

A captured comparison showed:

- Working V1 Kimi/GLM requests: every input item had `type: "message"`, with no `encrypted_content`.
- Failing V2 GLM request: the final input item had `type: "agent_message"`. Even when that captured request had no encrypted payload, Ollama Responses still could not process the non-standard item type.

External-provider routing itself works under V1. The important distinction is that the Multi-Agent version is selected and stored by the root task's first parent turn, then inherited by the whole spawned agent tree:

- If a fresh task sends its first message using a V1-capable parent model such as Luna, the root task resolves to V1 and every subsequently spawned agent also uses V1.
- Switching models after the first message does not change the already stored Multi-Agent version.
- Starting the task with a catalog-forced V2 parent such as Sol or Terra therefore keeps the whole tree on V2, including external-provider children.

This is related to, but distinct from, #33284. That issue concerns plaintext visibility to local hooks before execution. This issue concerns wire-format compatibility with non-OpenAI model providers after dispatch.

### What steps can reproduce the bug?

1. Configure an external Responses provider, for example an Ollama Responses endpoint, in Codex configuration.
2. Configure a native agent role in `~/.codex/agents/*.toml` whose `model_provider` points to that external provider.
3. Enable Multi-Agent and Multi-Agent V2.
4. Start a fresh task using a parent model for which the model catalog selects V2, and send the first message with that model.
5. Invoke `spawn_agent` for the external-provider role.
6. Inspect the request sent to the external Responses endpoint.

The child instruction is serialized as an input item resembling:

```json
{
  "type": "agent_message",
  "encrypted_content": "..."
}
```

or as a plaintext `agent_message` item. Ollama cannot decrypt the encrypted form, and its Responses implementation does not accept the `agent_message` item type in either form.

Disabling the `multi_agent_v2` feature flag alone may not avoid the issue when the model catalog forces V2 for the selected parent model.

The current workaround requires all of the following:

1. Create a new task.
2. Select a V1-capable parent model such as Luna before sending the first message.
3. Set `multi_agent = true` and `multi_agent_v2 = false`.
4. Keep using that task after its first turn has resolved to V1.

This makes the entire task and every child agent use V1. It is not a provider-specific fallback, and it does not allow an OpenAI parent to retain V2 while only an external-provider child uses a compatible transport.

Relevant implementation areas appear to include:

- `codex-rs/core/src/tools/handlers/multi_agents_spec.rs`
- `codex-rs/core/src/tools/handlers/multi_agents_v2.rs`
- `codex-rs/protocol/src/protocol.rs` (`InterAgentCommunication::to_model_input_item`)
- `codex-rs/core/src/client.rs` (Responses request construction)

### What is the expected behavior?

Multi-Agent V2 should remain usable when either endpoint in an inter-agent route uses a non-OpenAI provider.

The requested behavior is **not** to downgrade external agents to V1 inside an otherwise V2 task. The root task and the entire agent tree should retain V2 lifecycle and coordination semantics. Only the wire representation at a non-OpenAI provider boundary should be adapted.

A provider-aware compatibility behavior would be:

- Preserve the existing encrypted `agent_message` path for OpenAI-to-OpenAI routes.
- For a route involving a non-OpenAI provider, keep the task text plaintext and serialize the outbound instruction as a standard Responses `message` item, for example:

```json
{
  "type": "message",
  "role": "user",
  "content": [
    {
      "type": "input_text",
      "text": "..."
    }
  ]
}
```

- Apply the same provider-aware conversion to initial spawn instructions, follow-up/`send_message` instructions, and child return messages as needed.
- Preserve V2 lifecycle behavior such as task identity, graph state, wait, follow-up, and completion.
- Leave existing OpenAI-provider behavior unchanged.
- Allow catalog-forced V2 parents such as Sol or Terra to spawn explicitly configured external-provider roles without requiring the root task to start under Luna/V1.

### Additional information

The compatibility decision should be made using the actual caller and recipient provider identities, not only the parent model name.

The current Luna-first workaround demonstrates that the configured external provider and native agent role can function when the payload uses standard V1 `message` items. It also demonstrates why that workaround is insufficient: it disables V2 for the entire root/child tree rather than making V2 interoperable with external Responses providers.

issues.title: Remove the 60-second limit on blocking waits

labels.name: enhancement
labels.description: New feature or request

labels.name: tool-calls
labels.description: Issues related to tool calling

labels.name: subagent
labels.description: Issues involving subagents or multi-agent features

issues.body:
@etraut-openai

Please remove this guidance from the developer prompt for GPT-5.6 and GPT-6 Astra:

> Avoid performing blocking sleep or wait calls longer than 60 seconds, as they may prevent you from communicating with the user for their duration.

This turns every long-running command into a pointless polling loop. Chromium builds can take tens of minutes or hours, forcing the agent to make dozens of tool calls that report nothing beyond “still running." which is a waste of tokens and "burns time" (from the model's POV, it doesn't like making repeated tool calls due to "time limits"). 

It also harms subagent work. Repeated wait timeouts make parent agents impatient, leading to messages like “Send your concise final message now” while the subagent is still busy. This leads to suboptimal, rushed answers and the same aforementioned "burning time".

The wait tool supports up to an hour max duration. So why handicap the model in the developer prompt? In reality the model hardly sends messages to the `commentary` every sixty seconds when not waiting for long-running commands, so this guidance is genuinely just theater.

Furthermore because of this, the model will disregard instructions from the user to supply a higher wait as it has to comply with the higher-priority developer instructions.

There is an internal inconsistency between this and earlier guidance:
> If the user's request requires calling tools, start with a message in the `commentary` channel. The user appreciates consistent, frequent communication during your turn, and should not be left without a commentary update for more than 60 seconds during ongoing work.

The key words are "ongoing work". A build is not ongoing work. Waiting for a subagent to finish a complex, time-consuming implementation or investigation is not ongoing work for the main thread. When the agent is totally blocked by a long-running task, it should diligently wait.

This is overall terrible universal guidance. Please remove it.

Also I'm not only considering myself here. This is generally bad advice for the model regardless of which type of user is using Codex. Please don't be uncharitable and assume I'm only fitting this to my use cases, because I'm not.

Ideally I'd reverse the guidance and say avoid tight polling if you do not need interim progress, and maybe even send a message to the `commentary` channel before an expensive operation informing the user it will take time. An alternative is also removing the line altogether, which is also an acceptable solution.
