issues.body:
### Bug type

Behavior bug (incorrect output/state without crash)

### Beta release blocker

No

### Summary

A session's **machine-chosen** model-account binding (`authProfileOverrideSource: "auto"`) is fed into model-catalog evaluation as `preferredProfileId`. When the model is routed through a CLI backend that declares `strictSelectedProfile` — `claude-cli` — and that auto-selected profile is not the backend's native one, every Anthropic row is reported `available: false` / `unavailableReason: "missing-auth"`.

The credential is not missing. The Claude CLI is logged in and the same backend runs turns successfully in other sessions. The only thing "wrong" is that an unrelated provider's account happens to be the session's current *auto* preference.

User-visible result: the Control UI composer shows **"No provider credential is configured for this model. Set it up in Model Setup."** and refuses to send, and every Claude row in the model picker is disabled with "Sign in needed". Re-authenticating and restarting the Gateway change nothing.

### Steps to reproduce

Anthropic access is the Claude CLI subscription only (no provider-level API key); auth is surfaced as the synthetic profile `anthropic:claude-cli`. At least one other provider has a stored account (here: OpenAI, two OAuth accounts).

1. Route a Claude model through the bundled backend for agent `main`:

```json
{ "agents": { "entries": { "main": { "models": {
  "anthropic/claude-fable-5-1": { "agentRuntime": { "id": "claude-cli" } }
} } } } }
```

`claude auth status` → `{"loggedIn": true, ...}`.

2. Run a turn in some session while the agent default is an OpenAI model. The account resolver persists its choice into the session entry:

```json
{
  "authProfileOverride": "openai:<account>",
  "authProfileOverrideSource": "auto",
  "authProfileOverrideCompactionCount": 3
}
```

3. Switch the agent default model to `anthropic/claude-fable-5-1`.

4. Read that session's catalog:

```
openclaw gateway call chat.metadata --params '{"agentId":"main","sessionKey":"<key>"}'
```

5. Remove **only** those three `authProfileOverride*` fields from the session entry and repeat step 4. (No restart needed — the Gateway loads the entry per request.)

### Expected behavior

`authProfileOverrideSource: "auto"` is a preference, not a constraint. That is exactly why [`resolveSessionProfiles`](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/blob/v2026.9.3/src/gateway/server-methods/chat-metadata-runtime.ts#L181-L193) sets only `preferredProfileId` for it and reserves `pinnedProfileId` for explicit `user` / `user-link` choices.

A native CLI route whose own credential is present and usable should stay `available: true` when the selected profile is merely an auto preference belonging to a different provider.

### Actual behavior

Step 4, with the auto binding present:

```text
accountSelection: {"kind":"shared","authProfileId":"openai:<account>","source":"auto"}
anthropic/claude-fable-5-1  available=false  unavailableReason=missing-auth
anthropic/claude-fable-5    available=false  unavailableReason=missing-auth
anthropic/claude-opus-5     available=false  unavailableReason=missing-auth
```

Step 5, after clearing only the three fields — same config, same credentials, same Gateway process:

```text
accountSelection: {"kind":"automatic","label":"Automatic account selection"}
459 models, 0 unavailable
anthropic/claude-fable-5-1  available=true
```

Meanwhile the agent-scope call (`chat.metadata` without `sessionKey`) and `openclaw models list` both report those models as available/configured, and the backend demonstrably works:

```text
[agent/cli-backend] cli turn: provider=claude-cli model=claude-fable-5-1 durationMs=5023
```

**Root cause.** In [`evaluateCliRuntimeModelAuthAvailability`](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/blob/v2026.9.3/src/agents/model-auth-availability.ts#L144) the pinned and preferred profiles are collapsed into one value:

```ts
const selectedProfileId = ref.pinnedProfileId?.trim() || ref.preferredProfileId?.trim();
```

When the backend declares `strictSelectedProfile` ([`cli-backend-auth-policy.ts#L16-L19`](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/blob/v2026.9.3/src/agents/cli-runner/cli-backend-auth-policy.ts#L16-L19)) and the selected profile is not `anthropic:claude-cli`, the non-pinned branch returns the untouched provider-only `evaluation` ([#L194-L199](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/blob/v2026.9.3/src/agents/model-auth-availability.ts#L194-L199)):

```ts
return ref.pinnedProfileId
  ? evaluateProviderAuth(provider, { modelId: ref.modelId, requiredProfileId: selectedProfileId })
  : evaluation;
```

For Anthropic-via-`claude-cli` that provider-only evaluation has no credential evidence, so it settles on `available: false` / `missing-auth` and never reaches the prepared runtime-auth result below. The pinned branch is clearly deliberate; the fall-through for a **non-pinned auto preference** looks unintended — it lets a machine-chosen preference veto a route the user never constrained.

**No good in-product escape.**

- No RPC clears the binding. `sessions.patch` has no auth field, and `{"model": null}` clears the model override but leaves `authProfileOverride` in place.
- Selecting the native account (`sessions.patch` with `{"model":"anthropic/claude-fable-5-1@anthropic:claude-cli"}`) does fix Anthropic, but it stores `source: "user"`, i.e. a hard pin — and then *every other* provider in that session drops to `auth-failed` (`openai`, `github-copilot`, `kimi`, `minimax`, `zai`, `deepseek`, `google`). Verified: 18 rows, 15 unavailable. The user trades one lock for its mirror image.
- It recurs. The next turn that resolves an account on a multi-account provider re-persists the auto binding, so any session that runs on OpenAI silently loses the ability to switch to Claude again.

I worked around it by deleting the `source: "auto"` bindings straight out of `session_nodes.entry_json`, which restored "Automatic account selection" and full availability in all 71 affected sessions.

### OpenClaw version

2026.9.2 (3928bad). The cited code path is unchanged in v2026.9.3.

### Operating system

macOS 26.6.2 (arm64), Node v26.8.1

### Install method

npm (global), stable channel with automatic updates

### Model

`anthropic/claude-fable-5-1` (same for `anthropic/claude-fable-5`, `anthropic/claude-opus-5`)

### Provider / routing chain

`anthropic` via the bundled `claude-cli` agent runtime (subscription auth, synthetic profile `anthropic:claude-cli`). Other configured providers: `openai` (2 OAuth accounts), `github-copilot`, `google`, `kimi`, `minimax`, `zai`, `deepseek`.

### Additional provider/model setup details

Anthropic has no provider-level API key on this host — the Gateway reads the Claude CLI keychain credential (`[agents/auth-profiles] read anthropic credentials from claude cli keychain`) and exposes `anthropic` as `effective: {kind: "synthetic", detail: "Claude CLI native auth"}`.

`openclaw models status` reports `anthropic/claude-opus-4-8` as `indeterminate` ("Auth readiness could not be confirmed") rather than missing, which is consistent with the synthetic route being resolved only through the prepared runtime path.

### Impact and severity

Sessions become **unsendable**, not merely restricted: the missing-auth reason is used as the composer's `baseDisabledReason`, so the user cannot send anything until they discover the model picker and choose a different provider. The message points them at Model Setup, which is a dead end because nothing is actually unconfigured.

It triggers on an ordinary action — switching an agent's default model from one provider to another — and hits every pre-existing session at once. 71 sessions here, including pinned ones. For a user whose Anthropic access is the CLI subscription plus any second provider account, Claude becomes unselectable across the board.

### Additional information

A minimal fix would be to not degrade readiness when `ref.pinnedProfileId` is absent — let the native/prepared runtime result stand and treat a non-pinned auto preference as ignorable for a `strictSelectedProfile` backend. Alternatively, stop persisting an auto binding whose provider cannot serve the session's current model, or expose a supported way to reset a session to automatic account selection.

Possibly related: #137979 (Gemini CLI readiness masking a *rejected* explicit selection) is the mirror case — there native readiness is too permissive for an explicit selection, here it is too strict for a non-explicit one.

issues.body: ### Bug type Behavior bug (incorrect output/state without crash) ### Beta release blocker No ### Summary With Slack Agent View session status enabled, OpenClaw can complete a turn, finalize its Block Kit progress card, and deliver the final reply while Slack Desktop continues displaying the agent as working; restarting the Slack desktop client clears the stale indicator. ### Steps to reproduce 1. Run OpenClaw 2026.9.3 with Slack Socket Mode and the following progress configuration: ```json { "streaming": { "mode": "progress", "nativeTransport": true, "progress": { "style": "card", "nativeTaskCards": false, "commentary": false, "narration": true, "toolProgress": false, "maxLineChars": 400, "commandText": "status" } } } ``` 2. From Slack Desktop on macOS, send a thread request that produces a multi-step progress card. 3. Allow the turn to finish normally. 4. Confirm that the progress card shows every step completed and that the final assistant reply is visible. 5. Observe that the native Slack callout still says the agent “is working.” 6. Restart the Slack desktop application. 7. Observe that the stale working callout disappears. ### Expected behavior When the turn reaches terminal completion and the final reply is delivered, OpenClaw should transition the Slack agent session from `processing` to `active`, and Slack Desktop should promptly remove the working callout without requiring an application restart. Slack documents `active` as the state to set when an agent has finished and is ready for the next prompt: ### Actual behavior The observed turn completed successfully: - The Block Kit progress card displayed `3/3 complete`. - The final assistant response was posted. - OpenClaw session history recorded a terminal assistant response. - The session had no pending inputs. - Slack Desktop continued displaying the agent working callout. - Restarting Slack Desktop cleared the callout immediately. The restart result suggests that the server-side session may already have been `active` while the desktop client retained stale UI. The available evidence does not establish whether Slack missed the status transition event, OpenClaw's terminal status write failed silently, or the ordering of the final message/card/status updates triggered a Slack client rendering race. ### OpenClaw version 2026.9.3 (`1391f7c`) ### Operating system - OpenClaw gateway: Ubuntu 24.04.4 LTS, Linux 6.8.0-124-generic, x86_64 - Affected client: Slack Desktop on macOS; exact macOS and Slack client versions were not captured ### Install method npm global installation, launched as a systemd user service ### Model `openai/gpt-5.6-sol` ### Provider / routing chain Slack Socket Mode → OpenClaw Gateway → OpenAI → `gpt-5.6-sol` ### Additional provider/model setup details The model/provider is not believed to be relevant. The failure is in the Slack agent-session status/UI lifecycle after a normally completed turn. ### Logs ```shell # Sanitized gateway evidence from the affected turn 2026-09-09T01:42:35.460Z channels/slack delivered reply to channel: # Sanitized session-history evidence progress card: 3/3 steps completed assistant terminal response: recorded with runTerminal=true pending inputs: 0 No Slack session-status cleanup error appeared at normal log verbosity. The current Slack helper catches `agents.sessions.setStatus` errors, logs them only through verbose logging, and returns `{ ok: false }`. The terminal caller does not inspect that result or retry the transition: - - ``` ### Screenshots, recordings, and evidence Note that restarting Slack Desktop cleared the callout without restarting OpenClaw or sending another turn. ### Impact and severity - **Affected:** Slack Desktop users using OpenClaw's Slack Agent View session status with progress cards. - **Severity:** Moderate UX/reliability issue. Work completes, but Slack falsely indicates that the agent is still running. - **Frequency:** One confirmed occurrence on 2026.9.3; broader frequency is not yet established. - **Consequence:** Users cannot reliably distinguish completed work from a hung turn and may send duplicate prompts, attempt to stop an already-finished run, or restart Slack/OpenClaw unnecessarily. ### Additional information ### Duplicate and fix check Checked on 2026-09-08: - Latest stable release was 2026.9.3. - Searches of open and closed `openclaw/openclaw` issues found no report matching a Slack Agent View working callout that remains after successful completion and clears on desktop-client restart. - No post-2026.9.3 commit to the relevant Slack session-status or dispatch files was found. - Upstream `main` still performs a single `processing` write at turn start and a single `active` write during typing cleanup. Related but not duplicate: - concerned an older typing indicator persisting after an LLM timeout and rapid queued replies. - introduced the current Slack Agent View `processing`/`active` lifecycle and states that the loading state should clear when the turn ends. ### Suggested investigation 1. Record the response from the terminal `agents.sessions.setStatus(status: "active")` call at non-verbose diagnostic level when it returns unsuccessful. 2. Confirm whether the affected request returned `status: "active"` and `agent_status: "active"` or whether another agent/session state remained `processing`. 3. Add a bounded retry or reconciliation step when the terminal `active` write returns `{ ok: false }`. 4. Consider issuing the terminal status update only after the final Block Kit card update and final reply are acknowledged, or repeat the idempotent `active` write after both complete if Slack clients can miss the first transition. 5. Add an integration/trace case covering: progress card finalization → separate final reply → terminal session status → no lingering working UI.

issues.title: SQLite worker store hard limit MAX_STORES=64 degrades fleets with >64 agents (sessions unavailable, misleading doctor --fix hint)

labels.name: P1
labels.description: High-priority user-facing bug, regression, or broken workflow.

labels.name: impact:session-state
labels.description: Session, memory, transcript, context, or agent state can drift or corrupt.

labels.name: impact:ux-friction
labels.description: User-facing flow adds avoidable confusion or support burden without fully blocking progress.

issues.body:
## Environment
- OpenClaw: 2026.10.10-beta.4
- Node: v24.22.1 (WSL2)
- Fleet size: 92 agents, each with its own `openclaw-agent.sqlite` under `~/.openclaw/agents/<id>/agent/`

## Symptom
After gateway start, every agent DB beyond the 64th concurrently-open store fails admission with:

```
AgentDatabaseAdmissionError: Agent <id> (/home/openclaw/.openclaw/agents/<id>/agent/openclaw-agent.sqlite): SQLite worker store capacity reached
Sessions remain unavailable. Stop the Gateway, run "openclaw doctor --fix" to inspect and repair this agent database, and restart.
```

Observed impact:
- ~28 of 92 agents report "Sessions remain unavailable" continuously (cron maintenance, memory-core standing-intent maintenance, session registry all fail for them)
- `sessions.catalog.list` returns UNAVAILABLE → WebUI session sidebar is empty
- Hundreds of repetitions per hour in the gateway journal

## Root cause
`dist/sqlite-worker-store-*.mjs` (~line 981) hardcodes:

```js
const MAX_STORES = 64;
```

and rejects with "SQLite worker store capacity reached" when `clients.size >= MAX_STORES`. There appears to be no config field or env var to override it (docs are silent on this limit).

All agent DBs were current-schema and passed `integrity_check` — nothing was actually wrong with them, so the suggested `openclaw doctor --fix` repair path does not apply to this failure mode and is misleading for operators.

## Local workaround (works, but fragile)
Patched `MAX_STORES` 64 → 160 in `dist/sqlite-worker-store-*.mjs` and restarted: all 92 agents admitted, zero capacity errors since, sidebar catalog healthy again. The patch is overwritten on every update, so we re-apply it after each upgrade.

## Request
1. Make the SQLite worker store limit configurable (gateway config or env), or
2. Close idle stores dynamically (e.g., LRU eviction) so fleets with more than 64 agents work out of the box, and
3. Consider distinguishing "overloaded" capacity errors from corruption in the repair hint so `doctor --fix` is not suggested for this case.

issues.body:
## Environment

- OpenClaw **2026.9.3 (1391f7c)** via npm global install
- Node v26.8.1, Linux 7.0.0-31-generic (x64)
- User systemd service (`openclaw-gateway.service`), `Restart=no` drop-in
- Single `main` agent, single workspace
- Agent database: 327.4 MiB · 48 markdown files · 2290 chunks

## Symptom

Gateway becomes **unkillable** during a memory reindex. SIGTERM via `systemctl --user stop openclaw-gateway.service` is queued behind an in-flight synchronous SQLite transaction and never executes. `TimeoutStopSec=330` elapses, process stays in `Ssl` state, `systemctl --user restart` has no effect. Only a hard reboot via `sudo reboot` recovers the host.

The two 0-byte lock marker files (`*.reindex-lock.sqlite`, `*.generation-lock.sqlite`) **survive the reboot** and continue to block every subsequent reindex attempt, so the freeze will recur on the next LCM compaction cycle.

## Evidence

Lock files (after reboot, 4+ hours old):

```
$ ls -la ~/.openclaw/agents/main/agent/openclaw-agent.sqlite.{reindex,generation}*lock* *.writer*
-rw-r--r-- ... 0 Sep  8 23:20 .../openclaw-agent.sqlite.reindex-lock.sqlite
-rw-r--r-- ... 0 Sep  8 23:21 .../openclaw-agent.sqlite.generation-lock.sqlite
-rw-r--r-- ... 4096 Sep  9 01:43 .../openclaw-agent.sqlite.generation-writer.sqlite
```

WAL bloomed to **51 MiB** (normal: <1 MiB):

```
$ ls -la ~/.openclaw/agents/main/agent/openclaw-agent.sqlite-wal
-rw------- ... 51326992 Sep  9 02:59 .../openclaw-agent.sqlite-wal
```

Memory index never settled:

```
$ openclaw memory status
Memory Search (main)
Dirty: yes
Indexed: 48/48 files · 2290 chunks
Agent database: 327.4 MiB · WAL 48.9 MiB
```

Journal excerpt during the freeze window:

```
Sep 09 02:59:04 node[2115]: [sqlite/transaction] slow SQLite transaction hold
Sep 09 02:59:28 node[2115]: [sqlite/transaction] slow SQLite transaction hold
Sep 09 02:59:58 node[2115]: [sqlite/transaction] slow SQLite transaction hold
Sep 09 03:00:48 node[2115]: [sqlite/transaction] slow SQLite transaction hold
Sep 09 03:02:37 node[2115]: [sqlite/transaction] slow SQLite transaction hold
Sep 09 03:05:46 node[2115]: [sqlite/transaction] slow SQLite transaction hold
...
```

Gateway process state at freeze (after reboot, fresh PID 2115):

```
$ ps -p $(pgrep -f 'openclaw.*gateway' | head -1) -o pid,stat,wchan,etime,cmd
   2115 Ssl  ep_pol   11:04 node .../openclaw/dist/index.js gateway --port 18789
```

`Ssl` = interruptible sleep, but `ep_pol` shows genuine polling — SIGTERM queued but never delivered.

## Related upstream issues (same bug class)

| Issue | Match |
|---|---|
| [#140620](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/issues/140620) (P0) | session-transcript reconciliation stalls at 27/~1500 sessions, lock file left over, sudo reboot needed |
| [#136311](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/issues/136311) (P1) | gateway reacquires reindex lock on every start; 19 GB orphans |
| [#115908](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/issues/115908) (P1) | session transcript projection reconcile can livelock |
| [#119720](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/issues/119720) (P1) | synchronous agent persistence blocks Gateway event loop at scale |
| [#138474](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/issues/138474) (P1) | node:sqlite transactions + memory-worker lock spin freeze gateway 45-90s |
| [#134337](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/issues/134337) (P1) | memory_search dirty maintenance repeatedly full-reindexes |
| [#124788](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/issues/124788) (P0, closed) | event loop blocks ~100s every ~10 min |
| [#112758](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/issues/112758) (P1) | missing `mmap_size` and `cache_size` SQLite pragmas |

## Suggested fix

1. **Auto-release stale lock files on gateway start.** If `*.reindex-lock.sqlite` or `*.generation-lock.sqlite` is older than 30 minutes AND `fuser` reports no current holder, remove it before opening the database. This unblocks future reindex attempts. (See `openclaw-memory-recovery` skill.)

2. **Set SQLite PRAGMAs by default in `openclaw-agent-db-*.mjs`** (next to the existing `busy_timeout` line at ~line 603):
   ```js
   db.exec(`PRAGMA busy_timeout = ${OPENCLAW_SQLITE_BUSY_TIMEOUT_MS};`); // already done
   db.exec(`PRAGMA mmap_size = 268435456;`);   // 256 MiB  — addresses #112758
   db.exec(`PRAGMA cache_size = -64000;`);     // 64 MiB   — addresses #112758
   ```
   `mmap_size` and `cache_size` are persistent in the DB file, so setting once is enough; `busy_timeout` stays per-connection.

3. **Bump default `OPENCLAW_SQLITE_BUSY_TIMEOUT_MS`** from `5e3` (5s) in `openclaw-state-db-contract-DGtx5mf2.mjs:74` to `3e4` (30s) so contended transactions retry instead of erroring during memory reindex.

4. **Make reindex truly async.** The current synchronous-SQLite write path is what blocks the event loop. Async writes via `node:sqlite` async API or a worker thread would prevent the entire gateway from stalling.

5. **Expose `sd_notify(WATCHDOG=1)` from the gateway loop** so user-level systemd `WatchdogSec=` + `Restart=on-watchdog` actually works. Currently the gateway does **not** call `sd_notify`, so `WatchdogSec` always fires and causes an infinite restart loop — there is no graceful recovery path today.

## Workaround (until upstream fix lands)

```bash
# 1. Hard kill the gateway (SIGKILL — SIGTERM is queued behind the SQLite transaction)
pkill -9 -f 'openclaw.*gateway'

# 2. Verify no current holder on the lock files
fuser -v ~/.openclaw/agents/main/agent/openclaw-agent.sqlite.reindex-lock.sqlite
fuser -v ~/.openclaw/agents/main/agent/openclaw-agent.sqlite.generation-lock.sqlite
# Both must return empty

# 3. Remove stale 0-byte markers (NOT the 4096-byte .generation-writer.sqlite — active session)
rm ~/.openclaw/agents/main/agent/openclaw-agent.sqlite.reindex-lock.sqlite
rm ~/.openclaw/agents/main/agent/openclaw-agent.sqlite.generation-lock.sqlite

# 4. Restart gateway and force full reindex
systemctl --user start openclaw-gateway.service
openclaw memory index --force --agent main
```

- [registered message tools remain on the direct-name list](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/blob/f91bca9546f5a5cc59a801efe3592d6910a58d80/extensions/codex/src/app-server/run-attempt-tools.ts#L35);
- [catalog projection retains each entry's inputSchema](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/blob/f91bca9546f5a5cc59a801efe3592d6910a58d80/extensions/codex/src/app-server/dynamic-tool-catalog.ts#L68), while a `catalogMode: "direct-only"` entry can use the separate direct namespace, so the older blanket “root tool” description is not universal;
- [deferred-discovery guidance](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/blob/f91bca9546f5a5cc59a801efe3592d6910a58d80/extensions/codex/src/app-server/thread-prompt.ts#L118) still does not add the proposed independent-call batching/bounded-result instruction.

These are source observations, **not new live-model delivery or token-saving measurements**. Before any revival, the remaining proof must cover the actual current implementation: direct text delivery, deferred rich-action discovery/execution, rejection of invalid rich/routed direct arguments before preparation, and resumed-session behavior. The compact-default contract still needs the maintainer decision described in the durable review.

<!-- grynn-author-status:125314:2026-10-21 -->

---

## Historical report and measurements

## Summary

On the Codex app-server dynamic tool surface, the always-loaded `message` tool ships its full manager schema — every action, provider/target/thread routing, media, message management — into the prompt on every turn, although the dominant use is a plain text reply. Deferred-tool guidance also never tells code-mode-only models to batch, so they emit many single-call `exec` round-trips with unbounded output.

## Problem to solve

Fixed per-turn prompt token cost for every Codex-backed session, and avoidable model round-trips (latency is round-trips, not milliseconds).

## Proposed solution

When `message` is direct but loading is not fully direct, emit a minimal root spec (`action: "send"`, `message`, `final`, `replyTo`, `threadId`, `additionalProperties: false`) whose description points to the deferred `openclaw.message` for anything richer, and push the complete original spec into the namespace tool list with `deferLoading: true` so the full surface stays discoverable via tool search with unchanged runtime/policy semantics. Extend `buildDeveloperInstructions` to instruct batching independent calls into one `exec` (`Promise.all`) with bounded tool results.

## Alternatives considered

Removing richer actions from the tool entirely (loses capability); prompt-text-only guidance without the narrow spec (doesn't remove the schema cost).

## Impact

Per-turn prompt tokens drop for every Codex session; fewer exec round-trips from code-mode models.

## Evidence/examples

Implementation exists on a local branch touching `extensions/codex/src/app-server/dynamic-tools.ts` and `extensions/codex/src/app-server/thread-prompt.ts`.

## Do you plan to open a PR for this?

Yes

## Additional information

Model-facing schema/description change only; no config keys.

## Verified scope correction (2026-08-24)

The original “every turn / every Codex session” wording is too broad. Live and source measurements show that the registered ~86.4K-character catalog is a host-side searchable superset, not initial model-visible prompt text. The rich message manager (~12.17K characters) is deferred; the direct root reply wrapper (~764 characters) is visible only on attempts where that direct reply tool is admitted. The measured initially model-visible OpenClaw-owned schema surface was ~4.87K characters.

The remaining scope is therefore: reduce the direct reply schema cost on message-enabled attempts, avoid unnecessary repeated catalog construction, and provide bounded batching guidance. The linked PR still needs exact-head proof that a direct text send and deferred rich-surface discovery both work.

## Current scope — October 21, 2026

This umbrella now contains two upstream-resolved mechanisms and two remaining product proposals. Source inspection is pinned to `f91bca9546f5a5cc59a801efe3592d6910a58d80`; this is not a new live-Gateway test.

- **Automation run completion:** merged [#162481](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/162481) (`9f330efbe677`) adds the bounded, event-driven Gateway wait used by the tool. The current tool sends `waitTimeoutMs`, budgets the RPC for the wait plus enqueue time, and preserves the accepted acknowledgement when an outcome is unavailable. Main/same-session jobs avoid waiting behind their caller. I am not proposing the old parallel polling owner.
- **Cron terminal persistence race:** merged [#167524](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/167524) (`e04a6e175f77`) drains accepted exact-run terminal persistence before continuation sealing, including asynchronous session-key preparation registered by the Gateway subscriber. Current ready-phase rejection is intentional; our old late-ready-event exception should not be carried forward. This drain is ordering, not a guarantee that a failed database write succeeded.
- **Terminal paging remains absent:** the current `terminal read` still renders the full owned buffer, and its input schema has no cursor/page-size fields. The earlier anonymized 25,190-byte duplicate observation remains historical evidence; no fresh latency/token benchmark is claimed.
- **One-call inspection remains a separate proposal:** the tool exposes `get` and `runs`, not the proposed combined `inspect`. Its need and core-tool contract still require a maintainer decision.

Please retain the terminal-paging/inspection product decision, rather than treating the historical cron and completion-wait mechanisms below as current unfixed defects. No competing PR is being opened ahead of that decision.

<!-- grynn-author-status:125312:2026-10-21 -->

## Original report (historical; superseded where noted above)

## Summary

`terminal read` returns the entire buffer snapshot on every call, and the `automations` tool cannot wait for a run to finish or inspect a job in one round-trip.

## Problem to solve

An agent tailing a long-running command re-pays the full scrollback in tokens on every poll with no way to fetch only new output. An agent that enqueues an automation run must poll `cron.runs` in a loop; `get` + `runs` need two round-trips (latency is model round-trips). Two latent bugs sit in the same seams: the Codex outer watchdog applies a generic RPC timeout to a completion wait (aborting an admitted run before its runId returns), and a sealed `ready` lifecycle marker rejects the Gateway's asynchronous terminal cron event, stranding rows at `running`.

## Proposed solution

Cumulative UTF-16 cursor offsets on the terminal snapshot with `cursor`/`maxChars` params and `startCursor/cursor/endCursor/truncated/hasMore` in the result (surrogate-safe slicing, 32K default / 128K max). A shared `src/cron/run-wait.ts` (deadline-bounded exact-run wait + bounded result projection) used by a new `waitForCompletion`/`completionTimeoutMs` on the `automations` `run` action and by the CLI (replacing its duplicate loop), plus an `inspect` action fanning `cron.get` + `cron.runs` concurrently. Codex outer timeout becomes completion-aware.

## Alternatives considered

Streaming terminal output as events (bigger protocol change; paging solves the token cost now); agent-side polling helpers in prompt text (doesn't remove round-trips).

## Impact

Bounded token cost for terminal tailing; automations usable without polling loops; fixes the stranded-`running` and premature-abort defects.

## Evidence/examples

Implementation exists on a local branch touching `src/agents/tools/terminal-tool.ts`, `src/cron/run-wait.ts`, `src/agents/tools/cron-tool*.ts`, `src/gateway/terminal/`, `extensions/codex/src/app-server/dynamic-tool-execution.ts`.

Yes

Tool-schema changes only; no config keys.

Only compact, redacted `sessions tail` metric presentation remains here.

The typed, revocable host trajectory capability landed in #125941 (merged 2026-08-18, merge `5301fb5e7f3cbbfad9ff260c0179c7a209058b66`). The canonical capability is `params.hostCapabilities.trajectory`; do not introduce a parallel `trajectoryRecorder` API. The original capability request below is historical.

The remaining implementation is #125905 at `2b550fbc01ac643bc8f40fedccd2c0d0feb9a034`. Its October 4 review accepted real source-CLI → recorder → SQLite evidence, including sanitizer/truncation markers and explicit-versus-unknown byte counts, with no before-merge code findings. That supersedes this issue's older size-proof objection. Current conflicts and failed CI still require resolution; the accepted proof is not a claim that the PR is ready to merge.

Preserve the existing sanitizer boundary and distinguish original size from stored/sanitized size. No second capability or metrics implementation is needed while the linked PR is active.

## Historical report and earlier correction (retained verbatim)

## Summary

Two related observability gaps: `openclaw sessions tail` prints only bare event labels, and the harness trajectory recorder reaches plugins through an untyped cast that is never revoked at attempt settlement.

## Problem to solve

An operator debugging token burn, prompt bloat, cache breakage, or slow tools sees only "prompt submitted" / "context compiled" / "gpt-5 done" in the tail and must leave it to query SQLite manually — prompt/system/skill sizes, token usage, cache retention, tool result sizes, and durations are all invisible. Separately, harness plugins obtain the host trajectory recorder via `params as typeof params & { trajectoryRecorder?... }`, so the sink is outside the host-capability contract and is not revoked when the admitted run settles — a plugin could retain SQLite write access after its run ended.

## Proposed solution

Compact metric formatters in the tail renderer (`prompt=…ch`, `tokens(in/out/cacheR/cacheW/…)`, `retention=…`, `cacheBroke`, `result=…KB`, `duration=`), and a first-class `trajectoryRecorder` on `AgentHarnessHostCapabilities` wrapped by the same `assertActive()` revocation as other host capabilities; Codex reads it from `params.hostCapabilities` instead of casting.

## Alternatives considered

A separate metrics subcommand (rejected: the tail is where the operator already is); leaving the recorder cast in place (rejected: capability scoping is an ownership invariant, not a style preference).

## Impact

Debuggability of live sessions without SQL spelunking; plugin capability lifetime matches the admitted run.

## Evidence/examples

Implementation exists on a local branch touching `src/commands/sessions-tail.ts`, `src/agents/harness/host-capability*.ts`, `extensions/codex/src/app-server/*`.

## Do you plan to open a PR for this?

Yes

No new config; plugin SDK gains `hostCapabilities.trajectoryRecorder`.

## Current-main scope correction (2026-08-24)

Current `main` now provides and revokes the canonical typed `params.hostCapabilities.trajectory` capability. A parallel `trajectoryRecorder` plugin API is no longer needed and should not be added. issues.body:
### Bug type

Behavior bug (incorrect output/state without crash)

### Beta release blocker

No

### Summary

For a custom (non-built-in) ACP harness spawned through `sessions_spawn({ runtime: "acp" })`, OpenClaw pushes a `thinking` level it *derived itself* (`resolveThinkingDefault` → `"off"` when a `model` was given) as a hard requirement over `session/set_config_option`. If the harness advertises a `configOptions` list that does not contain `thinking` (or the `effort` alias), the whole turn aborts with `ACP_BACKEND_UNSUPPORTED_CONTROL` — even though the harness never claimed to support thinking, the value is the default, and the user asked for nothing.

The same happens for `model`: the brain passes its own resolved `provider/model` ref (e.g. `anthropic/claude-haiku-4-5-20251001`) as `sessions_spawn`'s `model` argument, and it is pushed at a harness whose advertised model list cannot contain it.

Net effect: a spec-conformant custom harness that honestly advertises the one option it has (a fixed `model` select) cannot be used from the gateway at all. The only way to make it work today is for the harness to advertise **no** config options (reply to `set_config_option` without a `configOptions` list), which is what we ended up doing.

### Steps to reproduce

1. Register a custom ACP harness in the acpx plugin (`plugins.entries.acpx.config.agents.myharness = { command, args }`) and an OpenClaw agent `{ id: "myharness", runtime: { type: "acp", acp: { agent: "myharness", backend: "acpx" } } }`. The harness (any minimal ACP agent over stdio) returns from `session/new` and from `session/set_config_option`:
   ```json
   {"configOptions":[{"id":"model","name":"Model","type":"select","category":"model","currentValue":"fixed","options":[{"value":"fixed","name":"fixed"}]}]}
   ```
   and accepts `set_config_option` for `model`.
2. `openclaw agent --agent myharness -m 'Use sessions_spawn with runtime "acp" and agentId "myharness" to delegate: reply with only the token OK.'` — the brain calls `sessions_spawn({runtime:"acp", agentId:"myharness", model:"anthropic/claude-haiku-4-5-20251001", …})` (it adds `model` on its own on most calls).
3. Observe the turn abort before `session/prompt`.

Also reproducible when the harness advertises **no** `configOptions` in `session/new` but echoes any list from `set_config_option`: acpx narrows its advertised set to that list and the next control (`thinking`) fails with `Supported config options: model` (or `none` if the list is empty).

### Expected behavior

- A `thinking` value OpenClaw derived by default (not user-requested) should be best-effort: skipped, or downgraded to a warning, when the harness advertises neither `thinking` nor `effort` — the way `timeout`/`timeout_seconds` are already tolerated (`isUnsupportedOptionalTimeoutConfigRejection`).
- Pushing OpenClaw's own `provider/model` ref at a custom harness whose advertised `availableModels` does not include it should not be fatal either (the harness's model is its own; the acpx CLI path already validates `--model` against the advertised list and refuses client-side, but the runtime path just sends it).

### Actual behavior

```
AcpRuntimeError: ACP session agent:myharness:acp:…:oneshot:… does not advertise config option 'thinking'. Supported config options: model.: code=ACP_BACKEND_UNSUPPORTED_CONTROL
```
and, when the harness advertises only `thinking`/`fast` and leaves `model` to the legacy `models` field:
```
AcpRuntimeError: ACP backend "acpx" does not accept config key "model". code=ACP_BACKEND_UNSUPPORTED_CONTROL
```
The brain then reports "The ACP harness session failed and produced no output to relay."

Where it happens (2026.7.1 dist): `applyManagerRuntimeControls` in `src/acp/control-plane/…` builds the pairs via `buildRuntimeConfigOptionPairs(options)` — `model` and `thinking` come from `resolveAcpSpawnRuntimeOptions` (`src/acp/spawn`), which sets `thinking = resolveThinkingDefault(...)` whenever a `model` is present — and throws `ACP_BACKEND_UNSUPPORTED_CONTROL` when `advertisedKeys.size > 0 && !advertisedKeys.has(key)`. acpx's side is `resolveSupportedConfigOptionId` in `src/runtime/engine/manager.ts`.

### OpenClaw version

2026.7.1-2 (0790d9f), `@openclaw/acpx` 2026.7.1 bundling acpx 0.11.2

### Operating system

macOS 15 (Darwin 24.5), Node 24.19.0

### Install method

npm (global), dev profile (`--dev`)

### Model

anthropic/claude-haiku-4-5 (the OpenClaw brain); the harness's own model is fixed server-side and not selectable

### Provider / routing chain

`openclaw agent --agent <acp-agent>` → OpenClaw brain (anthropic) → `sessions_spawn(runtime:"acp")` → acpx (embedded) → custom harness command over stdio

### Additional information

Context: the harness is `fountain acp` (https://github.com/BinaryBourbon/fountain, ADR 0015) — a remote-conversation ACP agent whose model is a property of the server-side agent, so per-session `model`/`thinking` genuinely do not exist. Full investigation with the acpx code paths: https://github.com/BinaryBourbon/fountain/issues/760 and PR https://github.com/BinaryBourbon/fountain/pull/767. Happy to test a fix against a live gateway.

A related but separate acpx report (one-shot `ensureSession` creating a second backend session per spawn) is filed on openclaw/acpx.

issues.body:
### What happened

`openclaw doctor` reports Telegram as unconfigured on a multi-account setup where every
account already defines `groups`, and group routing demonstrably works:

```
- channels.telegram: Telegram is in first-time setup mode. DMs use pairing mode, so new
  senders must start a chat and be approved before regular messages are accepted. Group
  messages stay blocked until you add allowed chats under channels.telegram.groups (and
  optional sender IDs under channels.telegram.groupAllowFrom), or set
  channels.telegram.groupPolicy to "open" if you want broad group access.
```

The bots in those groups reply normally, so the warning is a false positive.

### Reproduction

```json
{
  "channels": {
    "telegram": {
      "enabled": true,
      "dmPolicy": "pairing",
      "groupPolicy": "allowlist",
      "groupAllowFrom": ["11111111"],
      "defaultAccount": "default",
      "accounts": {
        "default": { "groups": { "-1001111111111": { "requireMention": true } } },
        "second": { "groups": { "-1002222222222": { "requireMention": true } } }
      }
    }
  }
}
```

Run `openclaw doctor`. The `channels.telegram` line appears even though both account
scopes are fully configured and neither of them warns.

### Root cause

Two layers, and the first one is the more consequential.

**1. `resolveDoctorChannelAccountIds` returns `undefined` for every channel during a real
doctor run.** It resolves the channel through `normalizeAnyChannelId`, which only knows
channels present in the plugin *registry*. Doctor inspects config without starting
channels, so that registry is empty. Measured on a real run with temporary instrumentation:

```
TMPDIAG2 channelId=null
TMPDIAG  telegram accountIds=undefined implicit=true active=6
```

Because `accountIds` is `undefined`, `hasImplicitActiveAccount` is unconditionally `true`
in `empty-allowlist-scan.ts`. That means **`suppressParentGroupAllowlistWarning` — added in
#93434 to avoid exactly this class of parent-scope false positive — is always `false` in
production.** Its tests pass because they run in a context where the registry is populated.

Note the inconsistency inside doctor itself: `channel-doctor.ts` finds the Telegram adapter
fine via `resolveReadOnlyChannelPluginsForConfig` (config-driven), so the *warning* is
produced, while `channel-capabilities.ts` needs the registry, so the data that would
*suppress* it is missing. `getDoctorChannelCapabilities` already dodges this by consulting
the bundled catalog first; `resolveDoctorChannelAccountIds` has no such fallback.

**2. The parent container scope is checked as if it were an account.**
`scanEmptyAllowlistPolicyWarnings` calls `checkAccount(channelConfig, "channels.telegram",
…, parent: undefined)`. With `accounts` in use that scope holds no `groups` of its own, so
Telegram's first-time guidance fires there while both account scopes stay silent. The
scanner's suppression signal is forwarded to `collectEmptyAllowlistPolicyWarningsForAccount`
but not to the channel-supplied `extraWarningsForAccount` hook, which is where that
guidance comes from.

Fixing only layer 1 leaves the warning in place; fixing only layer 2 is dead code, because
the suppression data never arrives. Verified by building the repo and running the real CLI:

| Applied | `first-time setup` warnings |
|---|---|
| neither | 1 |
| layer 1 only | 1 |
| both | 0 |

### Expected

No first-time setup warning on the parent scope when every active account configures
`groups`. Accounts that are genuinely unconfigured keep warning at their own scope, setups
with no `accounts` block are unaffected, and a container-level `botToken`/`tokenFile`/
`$TELEGRAM_BOT_TOKEN` (which synthesizes an implicit `default` account inheriting the
container) must keep its guidance.

issues.body:
## Current status and preferred contract — October 13, 2026

Source-only follow-up on [`605065ce7461`](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/commit/605065ce7461177e9b438c8d8917641a8e8380e0). The ordinary [dynamic-tool timeout resolver](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/blob/605065ce7461177e9b438c8d8917641a8e8380e0/extensions/codex/src/app-server/dynamic-tool-execution.ts#L393) still chooses explicit call arguments, selected built-in configuration, or the 90-second watchdog default, with a 600-second ordinary cap. Its owner-supplied execution-budget lookup is currently restricted to `node_exec`; dynamic MCP tools cannot supply their server budget there.

[PR #155490](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/155490) is merged and projects `requestTimeoutMs` to native Codex `tool_timeout_sec`. That improves the **native MCP route**, while requester-scoped servers still use dynamic tools and remain outside that projection.

Preferred direction: carry the effective owning MCP server's existing request budget into dynamic execution, without a second configuration knob or an `mfs_*` name-specific rule. Explicit call precedence, the bounded cap, abort propagation, and completion grace for a structured timeout result must remain explicit. The [current timeout reference](https://docs.openclaw.ai/plugins/codex-harness-reference/timeouts) defines separate inner/outer budgets, so inheritance needs an intentional maintainer contract decision before implementation.

No slow MCP operation was dispatched for this update; no new production timing is claimed.

---

### Summary

The Codex dynamic-tool watchdog uses one default timeout for every tool call. An MCP server that is legitimately slower than that default has its calls aborted even when the operator has already configured a longer `requestTimeoutMs` for that server — the two numbers never meet.

### Problem to solve

An operator configures an MCP server with a multi-minute request timeout because some of its operations genuinely take that long (one tool call fronting a bulk business operation). The MCP client honours it. The dynamic-tool watchdog does not, and kills the call at its own default.

The result is the failure class this repo ranks worst: the call ends with no useful outcome, and the model receives a timeout that says nothing about the server's real behaviour.

Before proposing new surface I checked whether existing behaviour can already express this, per the config-surface bar in AGENTS.md. In the current beta the watchdog resolves a configured value for exactly three tools — image generation, image, and message — through dedicated config paths. There is no generic per-tool or per-server path and no environment variable. The MCP client's `requestTimeoutMs` lives in the MCP runtime and is never read by the dynamic-tool module.

### Proposed solution

Preferred, because it adds **no** config surface: let the dynamic-tool watchdog derive its default from the owning MCP server's already-configured `requestTimeoutMs`. The operator has already stated the intended bound; the watchdog just needs to see it.

If that coupling is unwanted, a server-scoped or tool-scoped configurable default would also solve it.

Either way, explicit per-call timeouts should keep winning, and the existing hard cap should still bound whatever is resolved.

### Alternatives considered

Raising the global default — rejected, it weakens the watchdog for every fast tool to accommodate one slow server.

Patching the built watchdog — this is what we do today, and it is precisely what we would like to stop doing.

### Impact

Any deployment fronting a slow backend through MCP hits this. The workaround is a dist patch that must be re-derived on every upgrade.

### Evidence/examples

Reproduced on a six-agent fleet whose bundled MCP server routinely exceeds the watchdog default on bulk operations.

### Do you plan to open a PR for this?

Yes, if maintainers indicate which of the two directions is acceptable — I did not open one first because this touches config/default surface and reads as a product decision.

### Additional information

Filed with AI assistance; investigated and validated by me.

issues.body:
## Symptom
With `channels.feishu.streaming = { mode: "partial", block: { enabled: true } }`,
long agent replies that involve several tool calls sometimes end with **only** a
single card reading `⚠️ 🧰 Process failed` (or the failing tool's equivalent, e.g.
`⚠️ 🛠️ Exec failed`). The streamed answer text is gone — the whole card is just that one line.

## What "⚠️ 🧰 Process failed" actually is (corrected root cause)
It is **not** a generic core/Feishu error card. It is the **failure warning of a
specific tool**:
- `🧰` is the `process` tool's display emoji and `Process` is its title —
  `src/agents/tool-display-config.ts` (`{ emoji: "🧰", title: "Process" }`).
  The same format produces `⚠️ 🛠️ Exec failed` for the `exec` tool.
- The text is built by `src/agents/embedded-agent-runner/run/tool-error-warning.ts`
  (`formatToolErrorWarningText`, the `terminalDiagnostic.kind === "process"` branch)
  via `buildFailureWarning`. Format: `⚠️ ${toolLabel} failed (${reason})…`.
- This warning is **gated**: `resolveToolErrorWarningPolicy` returns
  `showWarning: !hasUserFacingReply` for `process`/`exec` failures. It is intended as
  the *last-resort* failure signal that only appears when **no other user-facing reply
  exists**. Its appearance as the sole visible content is therefore itself proof that the
  streamed answer was already lost upstream.

## Where the answer is actually lost
`extensions/feishu/src/reply-dispatcher.ts`:
- During a partial (non-block) stream, accumulated text lives in `streamText`, but
  `hasStreamingFinalText` stays `false` — it is only set `true` when a `final` payload
  arrives (line ~1416).
- When the run ends with an error `final` payload (the tool warning), the final-text
  merge at lines ~1265–1268 computes:
  ```ts
  mergeStreamingFinalText(streamText, warningText, payload.isError === true && hasStreamingFinalText)
  ```
  Because `hasStreamingFinalText` is `false`, `appendError` is `false`, so
  `mergeStreamingFinalText` returns **only the warning**, and the subsequent
  `streamText = text` overwrite (line ~1415) discards the accumulated answer.

## This is currently an intentional, test-encoded design
`extensions/feishu/src/reply-dispatcher.test.ts:1054` —
*"replaces a partial preview when the first final is an error"* — asserts that a partial
preview is discarded and only the error text is shown. The contrasting test at line 1018
shows the intended preserve-and-append behavior **only** works when a normal `final`
answer was delivered before the error. So this is a deliberate decision, not an oversight
— which is exactly why the beta1 → beta2 upgrade did not change the behavior.

## Repro
- Feishu plugin + core `2026.8.1-beta.2`
- `channels.feishu.streaming = { mode: "partial", block: { enabled: true } }`
- Send a query that streams a long answer and calls several tools
- Force a mid-stream failure (SIGTERM / timeout) on a tool — for the `process` tool this
  yields `⚠️ 🧰 Process failed (signal …)`
- Result: user sees only `⚠️ 🧰 Process failed`; the streamed answer is gone

## Expected (per the 2026.8.1 settlement mechanism)
On a mid-stream tool failure, `ensureVisibleStreamingDelivery` should send a static
fallback card containing the **accumulated streamed text + an error note**. The streaming
card should not be orphaned and the answer should not be replaced by the bare tool-error
warning.

## Actual
The streamed answer is dropped; the only visible content is the tool's failure warning
(`⚠️ 🧰 Process failed`).

## Suggested fix direction (requires a design decision)
In `extensions/feishu/src/reply-dispatcher.ts` (~line 1268), the `appendError` gate
`payload.isError === true && hasStreamingFinalText` should preserve a non-empty
`streamText` on an error `final`. `mergeStreamingFinalText` already guards the empty-
`previousText` case, so the `hasStreamingFinalText` conjunct is redundant and too narrow.
The now-misleading test at `reply-dispatcher.test.ts:1054` would need to be updated to
reflect the new (preserve-and-append) behavior, plus a regression test for a long partial
answer followed by a tool-error final.

---
Environment note: **Verified against the exact deployed version.** The mechanism was
confirmed present at identical line numbers in `v2026.8.1-beta.2` (commit
`b53e197f37cf1e42887c91a3003081bd74a17a34`) — the tag exists on the `upstream` remote
(`github.com/openclaw/openclaw`); the local `origin` is a fork (`wuruofan/openclaw`) that
had not fetched it. In both `beta2` and current `main` (`d5f41f734b2`) the same lines
apply: `extensions/feishu/src/reply-dispatcher.ts:1268`
(`payload.isError === true && hasStreamingFinalText`), `:1416`
(`hasStreamingFinalText = true`), and `extensions/feishu/src/reply-dispatcher.test.ts:1054`
(`replaces a partial preview when the first final is an error`). The `hasStreamingFinalText`
merge gate and that test case were introduced in `7cca3d4618b` (#94428, 2026-06-18).
All cited line numbers are exact for both `beta2` and `main`.

issues.body:
## Summary

`openclaw sessions list --json` reads the session store locally but does not project `archivedAt`, and it treats an unlocked historical `agentHarnessId` as the current runtime. The authoritative Gateway `sessions.list` projection reports both lifecycle state and the runtime that would handle the next turn.

This creates an operator-visible split brain: after a successful stock `sessions archive`, the CLI list still looks active; after changing the configured runtime, old unlocked sessions still look pinned to the historical harness even though the Gateway will use current policy.

## Reproduction

With current policy selecting `codex`, use an existing unlocked session that contains historical `agentHarnessId: openclaw`, then archive it:

```text
openclaw sessions archive <key> --json
# status: archived

openclaw sessions list --all-agents --limit all --json
# no archived field
# agentRuntime: { id: openclaw, source: session }

openclaw gateway call sessions.list --json \
  --params {limit:500,archived:all,includeGlobal:true,includeUnknown:true}
# archived: true
# agentRuntime: { id: codex, source: implicit }
```

Observed on the signed `2026.8.1-beta.2` build and confirmed by current-main source:

- `src/commands/sessions-table.ts` omits `archivedAt` from `SessionDisplayRow`.
- `src/commands/sessions.ts` passes the whole entry to `resolveModelAgentRuntimeMetadata`, which calls `resolvePersistedSessionRuntimeId` and treats historical `agentHarnessId` as current intent.
- the Gateway projection uses `resolveSessionRuntimeOverrideForProvider`; unlocked `agentHarnessId` is history, while only a compatible explicit override or locked transcript owns future runtime.

## Expected

The stock CLI inventory should expose archive state and report the same effective runtime semantics as the authoritative Gateway. Historical harness provenance should not be presented as an active pin for unlocked sessions.

## Why this matters

Operators use `sessions list` to choose lifecycle targets and diagnose routing drift. A false active/runtime inventory encourages unnecessary config changes and makes successful cleanup impossible to verify.

## Proposed minimal fix

Keep the local read-only list, but:

1. project `archived`/`archivedAt` from the existing entry;
2. resolve effective runtime with the same compatibility rule used by the Gateway: configured policy unless a compatible explicit override or locked transcript owns the session;
3. add parity regressions for archived rows, unlocked historical harnesses, explicit overrides, and locked ownership.

No new persistence, migration, background reconciliation, or configuration is required.

### Bug type

Behavior bug (incorrect output/state without crash)

### Beta release blocker

No

### Summary

The stock CLI can archive and delete sessions but cannot restore an archived session, even though the Gateway and Control UI support the inverse lifecycle operation.

### Steps to reproduce

1. Run `openclaw sessions archive <key>` for a non-main session.
2. Run `openclaw sessions --help` and inspect the lifecycle commands.
3. Observe there is no restore/unarchive command.
4. Sending new work to the fixed archived key is rejected with guidance to restore it first, but no stock CLI command can perform that action.

### Expected behavior

`openclaw sessions restore <key>` should invoke `sessions.patch` with the caller-observed `expectedSessionId` and `archived: false`, matching the existing Control UI lifecycle contract.

### Actual behavior

Headless operators must use raw Gateway RPC/UI or delete the session to reuse its routing key.

### OpenClaw version

Current `main` at `6f418b93c63`; also observed on signed npm `2026.8.1-beta.2`.

### Operating system

macOS 26 development reproduction; Raspberry Pi OS / Linux production observation.

### Install method

Source checkout and npm global.

### Model

N/A — deterministic session lifecycle operation.

### Provider / routing chain

N/A.

### Logs

```text
cannot pin an archived session; restore it first
```

### Impact and severity

Affected: CLI/headless operators.

Severity: medium; a reversible lifecycle action becomes effectively destructive from SSH automation.

Frequency: every archived session that must resume under the same routing key.

Consequence: operators resort to deletion or unsupported RPC calls, increasing data-loss and operational risk.

### Additional information

The Gateway protocol already documents and implements `sessions.patch` with `archived: false`; this is CLI surface completeness rather than a new storage or protocol capability.

issues.body:
## Summary

When two copies of the same plugin id are discovered, the `duplicate plugin id detected` warning **names the copy that won and omits the copy that lost** — and describes both sides by origin only, producing `global plugin will be overridden by global plugin`. The diagnostic object internally carries the overridden path in `source`, but `pushRegistryDiagnostics` drops it when rendering the config warning.

The result is a warning that tells the user something is wrong but not which file to remove. In our case it survived several restarts and one wrong remediation before we read the source to find out which of the two copies was actually being ignored.

There is a second, worse behaviour behind it: removing the losing copy can flip the warning into a **hard `invalid config` that persists after the files are restored**, and the documented re-sync command is itself gated behind config validity — so the user cannot get out of it except via `doctor --fix`, which recovers by rolling `openclaw.json` back to last-known-good.

Host: OpenClaw `2026.7.1-2` (0790d9f, current `latest`), macOS 26.6.1 arm64, node 22.23.1.

---

## 1. The warning omits the overridden copy

What the user sees:

```
Config warnings:
- plugins.entries.ekho-adapter: plugin ekho-adapter: duplicate plugin id detected;
  global plugin will be overridden by global plugin
  (/Users/me/.openclaw/npm/projects/<pkg>__openclaw-generation__g-cfa45e8c51f295dc/node_modules/<pkg>/dist/index.js)
```

Both sides are `global`, so the sentence carries no discriminating information, and the only path shown is the **winner** — the copy that is working correctly and must be kept.

The diagnostic object does contain the answer. Calling the registry directly on the same machine:

```js
import { t as loadPluginManifestRegistry } from '/opt/homebrew/lib/node_modules/openclaw/dist/manifest-registry--UiRn6nq.js';
const reg = loadPluginManifestRegistry({ config });
```

```json
{
  "level": "warn",
  "pluginId": "ekho-adapter",
  "source": "/Users/me/.openclaw/extensions/ekho-adapter/dist/index.js",
  "message": "duplicate plugin id detected; global plugin will be overridden by global plugin (/Users/me/.openclaw/npm/projects/.../dist/index.js)"
}
```

`source` is the overridden copy — exactly the file the user needs to act on — and it is never displayed. In `pushRegistryDiagnostics` (config io) the warning is built as:

```js
const message = `${diag.pluginId ? `plugin ${diag.pluginId}` : "plugin"}: ${diag.message}`;
```

`diag.source` is discarded.

The two candidates, dumped from `discoverOpenClawPlugins` on the same box:

```json
{"origin":"global","source":".../npm/projects/...__openclaw-generation__g-cfa45e8c51f295dc/node_modules/<pkg>/dist/index.js","packageName":"<pkg>","packageVersion":"0.4.1"}
{"origin":"global","source":".../extensions/<plugin-id>/dist/index.js","packageName":"<pkg>","packageVersion":"0.4.0"}
```

Same package name, different versions — so `isSameGlobalPackageDuplicate()` (which requires equal `packageName` **and** `packageVersion`) correctly declines to suppress. The warning is legitimate; only its wording is not.

**Suggested fix** — interpolate the overridden candidate and the versions, which are already in scope at the call site in `loadPluginManifestRegistry`:

```
duplicate plugin id detected; ignoring <overridden.source> (<name>@<version>)
in favour of <winner.source> (<name>@<version>)
```

and/or have `pushRegistryDiagnostics` append `diag.source` when present. Either alone makes the warning actionable.

## 2. Removing the losing copy can wedge the CLI

Sequence on a working box, all of it inside `~/.openclaw/extensions/<plugin-id>/`:

1. `mv openclaw.plugin.json openclaw.plugin.json.off` — a fresh registry computation stops reporting the duplicate, but `openclaw status` **still prints the warning** (the CLI's copy appears to come from the persisted plugin index, not a fresh scan). `openclaw plugins registry --refresh` does not clear it either.
2. `mv package.json package.json.off` — config now hard-fails:

```
OpenClaw config is invalid
  - plugins: plugin: plugin manifest not found: /Users/me/.openclaw/extensions/<plugin-id>/openclaw.plugin.json
```

3. Restoring **both** files does not clear it. The error keeps naming a manifest that is present on disk with its original mtime and size.
4. `openclaw config validate`, `openclaw status`, `openclaw plugins registry --refresh` and `openclaw doctor` all refuse or degrade. Notably `plugins registry --refresh` — the command the generated index file itself recommends ("Use `openclaw plugins registry --refresh`") — is gated behind config validity, so it cannot be used to repair index staleness.
5. `openclaw doctor --fix` recovers, but does so by restoring `openclaw.json` from last-known-good and writing the live file to `openclaw.json.clobbered.<ts>`.

Two problems here. A stale plugin-index snapshot outliving the on-disk change is a correctness bug on its own; and rolling back the user's config file is heavy collateral for what is a plugin-directory edit, on a config that was never modified (ours diffed byte-identical before and after, so nothing was lost — but that was luck, not design).

**Suggested fix** — invalidate/rebuild the persisted plugin index when a recorded manifest path no longer stats as recorded, and allow `plugins registry --refresh` to run when the only config issues are plugin-discovery-derived. It is the documented escape hatch and should not depend on the state it is meant to repair.

## 3. Minor: no cleanup path from a hand-installed copy to an npm-managed one

`openclaw plugins install <pkg> --force` installs into `~/.openclaw/npm/projects/...` and leaves an older copy in `~/.openclaw/extensions/<plugin-id>/` in place, warning about it forever. That directory is also where the plugin's runtime state lives (`resolvePluginInstallDir(pluginId)`), so users cannot simply delete it. A hint in the warning — "this copy is unmanaged; run `openclaw plugins uninstall`/remove its manifest, runtime state under this directory is preserved" — would close the loop.

## Impact

Cosmetically minor, practically not: the warning fires on every CLI invocation and every gateway start, and because it points at the wrong file, the natural remediation is to remove the copy that is actually in use. Following it further (step 2 above) leaves the CLI unusable with an error message that contradicts the filesystem.

issues.body:
### Summary

Outbound Signal attachments are handed to signal-cli as a **filesystem path**, which silently assumes the gateway and the signal-cli daemon run as the same uid. When they don't — a hardened deployment where signal-cli has its own service user — every generated image or video fails at the last hop, after appearing to work.

`extensions/signal/src/send.ts` (still current on `main`):

```ts
const resolved = await resolveOutboundAttachmentFromUrl(opts.mediaUrl.trim(), maxBytes, { … });
attachments = [resolved.path];
```

The path lives under `~/.openclaw/media/outbound`, which is `0700` and owned by the gateway user, so a signal-cli running as anyone else cannot traverse it:

```
Signal RPC -32603: Failed to send message: …/media/outbound/image-….jpg
  (Permission denied) (AttachmentInvalidException)
```

### Why the obvious workaround doesn't hold

Granting the signal-cli user traverse-only access to the chain does not survive: **OpenClaw re-asserts `0700` on `media` on every generation.** Measured directly — `0710` before a run, `0700` after — so any `chmod` is undone before the send, and a watcher would be racing it. The file itself is world-readable; the path is not.

### Suggested fix, which needs no signal-cli change

signal-cli's `send` already accepts a data URI in place of a path. From its own `--help`:

```
-a, --attachment       Add an attachment. Can be either a file path or a
                       data URI. Data URI encoded attachments must follow
                       RFC 2397. Additionally a file name can be added, e.g.
                       data:<MIME-TYPE>;filename=<FILENAME>;base64,<BASE64 ENCODED DATA>
```

So passing `data:<contentType>;filename=<name>;base64,<…>` instead of `resolved.path` removes the shared-filesystem assumption entirely — the bytes travel over the JSON-RPC connection that is already open. The `filename=` parameter also preserves the original name, which the path form does not always manage.

Base64 inflates the payload by about a third, so this may be better as opt-in (a `channels.signal.attachmentTransport: "path" | "inline"` style switch) rather than an unconditional change, especially for video against `mediaMaxMb`.

A narrower alternative would be a configurable outbound media directory, so an operator can point it somewhere both uids reach. That works but keeps the assumption; the data URI removes it.

### Why a deployment would separate the uids

Not an unusual setup: signal-cli's state directory *is* the Signal account — anything that can read it can send as that identity and deregister the number — so it is worth confining to its own service user with `StateDirectoryMode=0700`, separate from the process that runs model output and tools. Path-based delivery makes that split cost media support, which is a surprising trade to discover at the last hop rather than at config time.

The workaround available today is to run signal-cli at the gateway's uid, which is what we ended up doing, and it means the gateway can read the account key material.

### Environment

- OpenClaw `2026.7.1-2`, `@openclaw/signal@2026.7.1`, npm global
- signal-cli 0.14.7 under its own systemd unit, `--http 127.0.0.1:8081`, `apiMode: "native"`, `autoStart: false`
- Debian Bookworm (Raspberry Pi OS), arm64
- Verified against `main` at the time of writing: `send.ts` still passes `resolved.path`

issues.body:
## Summary

On a healthy, connected Matrix account, an agent bound to a **room** cannot be reached without an explicit `--session-key`. Session-route resolution appears to work for DM targets and fail for room targets, which makes room-bound agents effectively one-way: they can post, but nothing a human says in the room reaches them.

Version: `OpenClaw 2026.7.1 (2d2ddc4)`, Matrix channel via the bundled plugin, single account.

## Reproduction

With a Matrix account connected and an agent bound to a room:

```
openclaw agent --agent <agentId> --channel matrix --to '<roomId>' --deliver --message hello
```

Result:

```
GatewayClientRequestError: Unable to resolve a session route for channel "matrix"
```

The **identical** command with an explicit session key succeeds — the agent runs and the reply is delivered to the room:

```
openclaw agent --agent <agentId> --channel matrix --to '<roomId>' \
  --session-key 'agent:<agentId>:matrix:room:<anything>' --deliver --message hello
```

The same command against a **DM** target also succeeds without `--session-key`.

So the delivery path, the account, and the binding are all fine. What fails is deriving a session key for a room target.

## Why this is not a connectivity problem

`openclaw channels status --json` reports the account healthy while this is happening:

```json
"connected": true,
"healthState": "healthy",
"lastEventAt": 1786510916880,
"lastTransportActivityAt": 1786510916880,
"lastInboundAt": null
```

`lastEventAt` and `lastTransportActivityAt` advance as traffic arrives, but `lastInboundAt` stays `null` — indefinitely, across restarts. Room traffic reaches the transport and never becomes an inbound dispatch.

Messages in the room are readable the whole time via `openclaw message read`, so they are being received and stored; they are simply never routed to the bound agent.

## Impact

For a room-bound agent this removes the entire inbound half of the conversation. The agent can post (cron output, alerts, questions) and a human can read it, but replies go nowhere — so anything shaped like "agent asks a question, human answers in the room" cannot complete. Working around it means every inbound path has to synthesise its own session key, which reimplements the routing the gateway is supposed to own.

## Notes

- `null` here reads as "never", not "zero" — the field is what distinguishes a channel that received nothing from one that received traffic and dropped it, which is why it seems worth surfacing.
- Possibly adjacent to #92653, though that requests *choosing* the inbound session for cache sharing, whereas here no session is derived at all for rooms.
- Happy to supply logs, a redacted config, or run a suggested probe — this is reproducible on demand here.

issues.body:
## Bug type

Behavior bug (incorrect output/state without crash)

## Summary

When an agent session times out (or is otherwise terminated), any background `exec` processes spawned by that session's tool calls are not killed or cleaned up. They continue running as orphaned processes, holding resources (PTY sessions, file handles, memory) until the OpenClaw process eventually reaps them or they complete naturally.

## Steps to reproduce

1. Start an agent session.
2. In the session, call `exec` with a command that takes >15s to complete (e.g., a large build, a long-running test, or a pipeline script).
3. The `exec` tool returns with a status indicating the command is still running in the background (via the `process` tool infrastructure).
4. Allow the parent session to time out (e.g., hit `agents.defaults.timeoutSeconds`).
5. Observe that the background process remains alive after the session ends. The process is visible in `ps` with a parent PID of 1 (init) or the OpenClaw gateway, not the terminated session.

## Expected behavior

On session termination (timeout, abort, or normal close), the gateway should:

1. Enumerate all background `exec` processes spawned by the session
2. Send SIGTERM to each, followed by SIGKILL after a grace period
3. Close PTY sessions and file descriptors
4. Log the cleanup actions for observability

## Actual behavior

The session termination path cleans up the model call and the session record, but does not walk the tree of spawned child processes. The transcript records the background process's existence, but nothing acts on it at session end.

Evidence from a session transcript:

```json
{
  "type": "message",
  "role": "toolResult",
  "toolName": "exec",
  "content": "Command still running (session <process-session-name>, pid <pid>). Use process (list/poll/log/write/send-keys/submit/paste/kill/clear/remove) for follow-up."
}
```

This tool result appears at the end of the session's transcript. The session status was `"timeout"` and `endedAt` was set, but the referenced process remained alive after the session record was closed.

Evidence from the gateway source: the `buildTimeoutAbortSignal` function creates an abort signal for the model call timeout, but the signal is scoped to the model invocation only. There is no cleanup path that walks spawned `exec` children:

```javascript
const { signal, cleanup } = buildTimeoutAbortSignal({
  // ...
});
// ... model call ...
cleanup();
```

No equivalent cleanup for background exec processes spawned via the `exec` tool during the session.

## OpenClaw version

2026.7.1-2 (0790d9f)

## Operating system

Linux 6.8.0-137-generic (x86_64)

## Install method

npm global

## Model

zai/glm-5.2 (primary), minimax/MiniMax-M3 (fallback)

## Provider / routing chain

openclaw → z.ai API (openai-completions compatible)

## Additional provider/model setup details

The `exec` tool's behavior when a command exceeds the default timeout is to return a "still running" message and assign a `process` session (auto-generated short name) and PID. These process sessions persist in the OpenClaw process table until explicitly cleaned up.

## Logs

Transcript evidence (last tool result before session timeout):

```
{"type":"toolResult","toolName":"exec","content":"Command still running (session <process-session-name>, pid <pid>). Use process (list/poll/log/write/send-keys/submit/paste/kill/clear/remove) for follow-up."}
```

Session termination record:

```
session.ended → <epoch-ms>
status        → "timeout"
```

No subsequent log entry for the orphan process cleanup. Post-hoc `ps` observation confirmed the process remained alive after the session record was closed (cleaned up later by an incidental system event, not the gateway).

## Impact and severity

- **Affected:** Any agent session that runs background `exec` commands (builds, tests, long-running scripts)
- **Severity:** Medium — resource leak; potential memory/PTY exhaustion over many timed-out sessions
- **Frequency:** Intermittent (only when sessions time out while background exec is running, or when sessions end normally with orphaned background processes)
- **Consequence:** Accumulating orphan processes over time. Each holds a PTY, file descriptors, and memory. In long-running deployments, this can exhaust process limits or PTY slots.

## Additional information

**Recommendation:** Implement session-scoped process tracking:

1. Tag each `exec`-spawned process with a `parentSessionId` at creation time.
2. On session end (timeout, abort, or normal close), iterate over child processes for that session.
3. Send SIGTERM, wait grace period, send SIGKILL.
4. Close associated PTY sessions and clean up the `process` tool's session records.
5. Log cleanup actions with the session ID for observability.

The `process` tool already tracks spawned processes by auto-generated session name. The gateway could maintain a reverse index from `parentSessionId` to `processSessionName` to enable this cleanup.

## Summary

`sessions.patch` silently drops `toolOverrides.webSearch: true` during normalize, so a session-level **enable** override cannot persist. `webSearch: false` already persists, and sibling boolean maps (`skills`, `mcpServers`) already keep `true`.

```json
{ "key": "agent:main:main", "toolOverrides": { "webSearch": true, "skills": { "docs": true } } }
```

succeeds, but the stored entry keeps `skills.docs: true` and **omits** `webSearch`. A lone `{ "webSearch": true }` normalizes to an empty overlay (`undefined`).

## Expected

`typeof webSearch === "boolean"` values persist (both `true` and `false`), matching `skills` / `mcpServers` boolean-map behavior. Control UI already emits `webSearch: true` when the global base is off (`nextWebSearchToolOverrides(..., true, false)`).

## Anchors (pre-fix)

- `src/gateway/sessions-patch.ts` `normalizeSessionToolOverrides`: previously `raw.webSearch === false ? { webSearch: false } : {}`
- Schema allows boolean: `packages/gateway-protocol/src/schema/sessions-row.ts` (`SessionToolOverridesSchema.webSearch`)
- UI intent: `ui/src/lib/sessions/tool-overrides.ts` (`nextWebSearchToolOverrides`)

## Impact

When `tools.web.search.enabled` is false (or the composer base is off), toggling web search **on** for one session appears to succeed over RPC but does not stick on read-back. Deny (`false`) works; enable (`true`) is a silent no-op.

## Repro

1. Call `sessions.patch` with `toolOverrides: { webSearch: true }`.
2. Read the session entry / list row.
3. Observe `toolOverrides.webSearch` missing (or entire overlay absent).

## Notes

Out of scope for this issue: whether the agent runtime honors a persisted `webSearch: true` against a global config disable (separate follow-up). This tracks **persistence/normalize** only.
