issues.body:
### Affected component

security/sandbox

### Severity

S0 - data loss / security risk

Conditional authorization-policy mismatch affecting an authenticated principal that already holds SOP execution permission. The agent's own security policy and SOP approval gates still apply.

### Current behavior

A non-admin principal with `sops = ["execute"]`, an allowed agent alias, and `allowed_tools = ["*"]` passes the SOP execution guard even when `tools = ["execute"]` is absent or has been revoked. An existing headless procedure can then run with its agent's tools. The same grant set produces an empty tool ceiling for an interactive session.

This is a source-confirmed finding at `73e2a4a15ddbdb01ffb4a044dc6c5c8dd7835110`; no runtime reproduction was performed.

- [The shared session ceiling](https://github.com/zeroclaw-labs/zeroclaw/blob/73e2a4a15ddbdb01ffb4a044dc6c5c8dd7835110/crates/zeroclaw-runtime/src/rpc/dispatch.rs#L490-L508) checks admin, then `Tools:Execute`, then the selector.
- [The SOP guard](https://github.com/zeroclaw-labs/zeroclaw/blob/73e2a4a15ddbdb01ffb4a044dc6c5c8dd7835110/crates/zeroclaw-runtime/src/rpc/dispatch.rs#L8167-L8181) accepts admin or a wildcard selector without checking `Tools:Execute`. Both [sops/run](https://github.com/zeroclaw-labs/zeroclaw/blob/73e2a4a15ddbdb01ffb4a044dc6c5c8dd7835110/crates/zeroclaw-runtime/src/rpc/dispatch.rs#L8312) and [sops/decide](https://github.com/zeroclaw-labs/zeroclaw/blob/73e2a4a15ddbdb01ffb4a044dc6c5c8dd7835110/crates/zeroclaw-runtime/src/rpc/dispatch.rs#L8554) reach that guard through `authorize_sop_agents`.
- [The headless executor](https://github.com/zeroclaw-labs/zeroclaw/blob/73e2a4a15ddbdb01ffb4a044dc6c5c8dd7835110/crates/zeroclaw-runtime/src/sop/executor.rs#L897-L915) supplies the procedure's security and step scope, without the RPC principal's tool ceiling.

Found during retrospective review of merged #10263. The omission existed in its predecessor's wildcard check and remains after #10265; this report is a follow-up, not a claim that #10263 introduced a new privilege escalation. Related #8289 and #7141.

### Expected behavior

SOP execution and approval should reject this grant combination. The [authentication contract](https://github.com/zeroclaw-labs/zeroclaw/blob/73e2a4a15ddbdb01ffb4a044dc6c5c8dd7835110/docs/book/src/security/authentication.md#L33-L35) says SOP execution uses the same tool-selector rule as sessions; [the session rule](https://github.com/zeroclaw-labs/zeroclaw/blob/73e2a4a15ddbdb01ffb4a044dc6c5c8dd7835110/docs/book/src/security/authentication.md#L192-L195) requires the coarse tool grant even with a wildcard.

Reuse `principal_tool_ceiling(&auth.grants).is_none()` for the SOP guard. Preserve the existing refusal of constrained SOP callers until the executor can carry their ceiling. Add focused run/decision coverage for wildcard without `Tools:Execute`, including revocation, and retain permitted-wildcard and admin controls. This does not require a new principal-propagation mechanism through the SOP engine.

### Steps to reproduce

```bash
# Source inspection, from a checkout containing this revision:
git show 73e2a4a15ddbdb01ffb4a044dc6c5c8dd7835110:crates/zeroclaw-runtime/src/rpc/dispatch.rs | sed -n '490,508p;8167,8181p'

# Runtime regression scenario to implement; not executed for this report:
# 1. Bind a non-admin synthetic principal whose profile has:
#    allowed_agents = ["test-agent"]
#    allowed_tools = ["*"]
#    [permission_profiles.sop_runner.grants]
#    sops = ["execute"]
#    No tools = ["execute"] grant.
# 2. Provide an existing SOP for test-agent with a permitted tool-using step.
# 3. Invoke sops/run for that SOP through authenticated RPC.
# 4. Verify refusal before dispatch; the current guard instead accepts it.
# 5. Cover the same grant combination for an approving sops/decide call.
# 6. Repeat after revoking only Tools:Execute from a previously permitted
#    profile, leaving the wildcard selector and Sops:Execute intact.
```

### Impact

Deployments using separate SOP and tool grants cannot rely on removing `Tools:Execute` to stop this SOP execution route. An authenticated caller still needs `Sops:Execute`, access to every relevant agent, an existing procedure, and any procedure-specific approval requirements. This is not an unauthenticated route. The existing warning about daemon-account execution remains relevant; this report concerns the narrower documented grant check.

### Logs / stack traces

```text
No runtime execution or logs collected; evidence is the source path linked above.
```

### ZeroClaw version

`master` at `73e2a4a15ddbdb01ffb4a044dc6c5c8dd7835110`; also present at #10263's final head `2b5f38118c15ffd4ef277ffcf4ea8651f00c8398`.

### Rust version

_No response_ — source review only; no build performed.

### Operating system

Platform-independent RPC authorization logic; no operating-system runtime reproduction performed.

### Regression?

Unknown. The omission is inherited from the earlier SOP wildcard check; no previously correct release has been established.

### Pre-flight checks

- [ ] I reproduced this on the latest master branch or latest release.
- [X] I redacted secrets, tokens, and personal data from all submitted content.

The first item remains unchecked because current-master source was inspected, but no runtime reproduction was performed.

issues.body:
The SOP workshop tool lets an agent write a new procedure into the shared procedures folder and load it right away. A limited user whose agent has this tool can write a procedure that an administrator or a scheduled trigger later runs with full power, even though the author had only limited power. This was only mentioned in a comment on a pull request, so the maintainers have not yet decided whether it is a bug or intended, and it needs its own issue.

### Affected component

security/sandbox

### Severity

S0 - data loss / security risk

### Current behavior

`sop_workshop` is registered for every agent when `[sop] procedural_memory_enabled` is on (`crates/zeroclaw-runtime/src/tools/mod.rs:2763-2771`), and it does not override `requires_unrestricted_principal`, so a non-admin principal keeps it. Its `apply` action calls `apply_proposal`, which writes SOP.toml and SOP.md under `<install>/shared/sops` and reloads the engine (`crates/zeroclaw-runtime/src/tools/sop_workshop.rs:273-280`). Nothing on that path checks who the principal is or whether they hold any `sops` grant.

### Expected behavior

Writing a shared procedure is SOP authoring, which over RPC requires `Sops` create or update grants (`crates/zeroclaw-runtime/src/rpc/dispatch.rs:509-510`). The tool path should enforce the same boundary, either by withholding `sop_workshop` from non-admin principals or by checking the caller's grants before `apply`. If the tool stays available to scoped principals, `apply` should refuse while read-only actions such as `list` and `inspect` keep working.

### Steps to reproduce

```text
1. Enable [sop] procedural_memory_enabled and configure a non-admin profile with sessions,
   tools = ["execute"], allowed_tools = ["*"], and no sops grant.
2. Open an OIDC-scoped chat on an agent and have it call sop_workshop with propose, then apply.
3. A new SOP appears under the shared SOP directory and is live after the reload; an administrator
   or a trigger can run it later with the agent's full tool set.
Source-traced at master 5d4b18d335; not executed.
```

### Impact

A scoped user can plant a procedure that administrators and headless triggers later execute with operator authority and the agent's full tool set. The procedure carries none of the author's grants or tool ceiling, so a limited account becomes a persistent escalation path. The gap was reported only as a review comment on PR #11410 (2026-10-12); it shares a root cause with #12046 and belongs under tracker #8289.

### Logs / stack traces

_No response_

### ZeroClaw version

master 5d4b18d335 (v0.8.7)

### Rust version

n/a (source review); CI pins 1.98.0

### Operating system

Any; reviewed in source on macOS

### Regression?

No, first-time setup

### Pre-flight checks

- [ ] I reproduced this on the latest master branch or latest release.
Source-traced at master 5d4b18d335; no runtime reproduction was run.
- [X] I redacted secrets, tokens, and personal data from all submitted content.

### Recommended action

Decide whether SOP authoring through the workshop tool is allowed for scoped principals at all; the safest answer is no. Mark `sop_workshop` as requiring an unrestricted principal so the existing registry filter removes it, and add a regression test that a constrained session cannot apply a proposal. If a read-only subset is wanted later, gate `apply` behind the caller's `Sops` grants in a follow-up.

issues.title: [Bug]: the plugin store limiter caps each linear memory at `max_memory_mb` and instances at 64 but keeps wasmtime's defaults of 10,000 memories and 10,000 tables per store, so a plugin can commit thousands of times its memory budget

labels.name: bug
labels.description: Something isn't working

labels.name: security
labels.description: Auto scope: src/security/** changed.

labels.name: runtime:wasm
labels.description: Auto module: runtime/wasm changed.

labels.name: domain:security
labels.description: Security domain

labels.name: topic:plugins
labels.description: Plugin capability catalog and lifecycle; former milestone #21.

issues.body:
### Affected component plugins ### Severity S2 - degraded behavior ### Current behavior Each plugin store is built with `StoreLimitsBuilder::new().memory_size(spec.limits.max_memory_bytes).table_elements(spec.limits.max_table_elements).instances(spec.limits.max_instances)` (`crates/zeroclaw-plugins/src/component.rs:297-301`), with defaults of 256 MiB, 100,000 elements and 64 instances (`crates/zeroclaw-config/src/schema.rs:9957-9975`). Those three settings bound the size of one memory, the size of one table and the number of core instances. They do not bound how many memories or tables a store may hold, and wasmtime's `ResourceLimiter` fills those in with `DEFAULT_MEMORY_LIMIT = 10000` and `DEFAULT_TABLE_LIMIT = 10000` (`wasmtime-48.0.8/src/runtime/limits.rs:3-8`). `memory_size` is consulted per memory as it grows, so the effective ceiling on a store is the number of memories times 256 MiB. Multiple memories per module are reachable because the engine is configured as `Config::new()` with fuel metering and nothing else (`component.rs:710-711`), and wasmtime enables the multi-memory proposal by default (`wasmtime-48.0.8/src/config.rs:1206-1209`, "This is `true` by default"). A component whose core module declares, say, sixty-four memories and grows each to the limit commits sixteen gibibytes while every individual check passes; sixty-four instances each with a handful of memories reach the same place; and the table side allows 10,000 tables of 100,000 elements each. Fuel and the call timeout bound compute, but growing memory is cheap and the allocation lands before either intervenes. ### Expected behavior The builder also sets `.memories(n)` and `.tables(n)` with small values (one or two per instance is enough for current plugins), or the store carries a `ResourceLimiter` that budgets total committed bytes across all memories and tables so that `max_memory_mb` means what an operator reads it to mean. A test loads a component that declares two memories and asserts that the second cannot grow the store past the configured budget. ### Steps to reproduce ```bash # Build a component whose core module declares two memories and grows both to the maximum # (wat: (memory 0 4096) (memory 0 4096) with memory.grow calls on each), package it as a plugin, # install and invoke it; watch the daemon's RSS pass 2 x max_memory_mb with no limiter error. # Scale the memory count to see the ceiling move with it. ``` ### Impact The actor is a plugin the operator installed, so this is a supply-chain and robustness concern rather than a remote one: a malicious package from a registry, a compromised update of a trusted plugin, or an honest plugin with a runaway allocation takes the daemon down with it, and with it every channel and agent the daemon hosts. The likelihood is moderate; plugins are the project's extension mechanism and the registry is open. Nothing is disclosed; the loss is availability and the false assurance the memory limit gives when a plugin is reviewed. **Data flow** ```mermaid flowchart LR L["StoreLimitsBuilder:
memory_size 256 MiB (per memory)
table_elements 100k (per table)
instances 64"] --> S["store"] D["wasmtime defaults left in place:
memories 10000, tables 10000"] --> S F["engine Config::new():
multi-memory enabled by default"] --> P["plugin module declares N memories"] P --> S S --> R["committed = N x 256 MiB, up to the 10000-memory ceiling"] classDef bad fill:#fde2e2,stroke:#b00000,color:#000 class D,R bad ``` **Evidence:** static review of master `1c1cd118ac` and the vendored wasmtime 48.0.8 sources; not executed. ### Logs / stack traces _No response_ ### ZeroClaw version master `1c1cd118ac` (v0.8.7) ### Rust version 1.98.0 (CI toolchain) ### Operating system any ### Regression? Unknown ### Pre-flight checks - [ ] I reproduced this on the latest master branch or latest release. - [x] I redacted secrets, tokens, and personal data from all submitted content.

issues.body:
## Task

Stop `cron update` from silently discarding changes to a declarative (`source = "declarative"`) job. Six columns are affected today: `command`, `name`, `expression`/`schedule`, `session_target`, `allowed_tools` and `uses_memory`.

Either reject them at `update_job` with a message naming the owning config key, matching the `delivery` and `shell_output_format` guards already there, or update the canonical config instead. A regression should cover the startup-sync boundary.

## Context

Surfaced during review of #9350. That PR added `delivery` to the same trap and guarded it; this issue covers the rest, which predate it.

A `[cron.<id>]` job is owned by `config.toml` and materialized with `source = "declarative"`. `update_job` persists a patch for such a row and reports success:

```rust
// crates/zeroclaw-runtime/src/cron/store.rs, update_job
if job.source == "declarative" {
    conn.execute(
        "UPDATE cron_jobs
         SET expression = ?1, command = ?2, schedule = ?3, job_type = ?4, prompt = ?5, name = ?6,
             session_target = ?7, model = ?8, enabled = ?9, delivery = ?10, delete_after_run = ?11,
             allowed_tools = ?12, next_run = ?13, uses_memory = ?14
         WHERE id = ?15",
```

`sync_declarative_jobs` then rewrites every one of those columns from the canonical `CronJobDecl` on the next daemon start, in both the schedule-changed and unchanged branches:

```sql
UPDATE cron_jobs
   SET expression = ?1, command = ?2, schedule = ?3, job_type = ?4,
       prompt = ?5, name = ?6, session_target = ?7, model = ?8,
       enabled = ?9, delivery = ?10, delete_after_run = ?11,
       allowed_tools = ?12, source = 'declarative', uses_memory = ?13
 WHERE id = ?14
```

So the CLI reports success, the row changes, and the change disappears at the next restart, reverting to the config value. The user gets no signal at any point.

The only production caller of `sync_declarative_jobs` is the scheduler's daemon-startup path, which is why this is invisible in a single session and only shows up after a restart.

**Two columns are already guarded**, and they establish the pattern this issue asks to extend:

- `shell_output_format` bails with "owned by config.toml for a declarative job, not the database".
- `delivery` bails with the owning key, added in #9350.

The comment on the first states the intent directly: `update_job` is "the core boundary every caller of `update_job` goes through, so it must reject them too rather than silently ignoring or persisting a value execution never consumes."

## Affected flags

Reachable today via `zeroclaw cron update <declarative-id>`:

| Flag | Column |
|---|---|
| `--command` | `command` |
| `--name` | `name` |
| `--expression`, `--tz` | `expression`, `schedule` |
| `--allowed-tool` | `allowed_tools` |
| `--uses-memory` | `uses_memory` |

`model`, `session_target`, `prompt`, `enabled` and `delete_after_run` are in the same UPDATE and would be reverted identically if a caller patched them, though the CLI does not currently expose all of them.

## Acceptance criteria

- A `cron update` that would change a config-owned column on a declarative job fails with a non-zero exit and an error naming the specific `[cron.<id>]` key, rather than persisting a value the next sync discards.
- Imperative jobs are unaffected; an update that sets none of the affected fields still succeeds on a declarative job.
- Store-level regressions per field, following `update_job_rejects_delivery_for_declarative_job`, which asserts the rejection and then runs `sync_declarative_jobs` to demonstrate the revert being prevented.
- At least one binary-boundary regression. Note that no CLI command runs `sync_declarative_jobs` — the only production caller is the scheduler's daemon start — so a component test has to seed the declarative row through the library, as `tests/component/cron_delivery_cli.rs` and `zeroclaw-gateway`'s own declarative test both do.

## Likely files or areas

- `crates/zeroclaw-runtime/src/cron/store.rs` — `update_job` (existing guards are the model), and `sync_declarative_jobs` for the revert behaviour.
- `src/cron/mod.rs` — the `Update` command arm, if the maintainers prefer an earlier, friendlier failure.
- `tests/component/cron_delivery_cli.rs` — existing harness with a declarative seed helper.

## Mentor, reviewer, or contact

@Audacity88 and @IftekharUddin, both of whom reviewed #9350 where this surfaced. @IftekharUddin asked for the deferral to be tracked here rather than left as an offer in that thread (FND-005 §5).

## Risk notes

Behaviour change: commands that currently appear to succeed would start failing. That is the point — they were never actually taking effect — but it is user-visible and belongs in the compatibility section of whatever PR implements it. Confined to the cron store boundary; no schema change, no migration.

Deciding between "reject" and "write through to config.toml" is worth settling before implementation. Rejecting is consistent with the two existing guards and much smaller; writing through would make the CLI a config editor, which is a larger design question.

issues.title: [Bug]: cron update --agent reports success but never reassigns the job's agent
issues.body:
### Affected component

runtime/daemon

### Severity

S2 - degraded behavior

### Current behavior

`zeroclaw cron update <id> --agent <alias>` accepts the flag, validates that the alias exists (`require_configured_agent`), prints the success block (`cli-cron-updated`, next run, payload confirmation) — but the job keeps executing under its previous agent. The reassignment is silently dropped.

Root cause: `CronJobPatch` (`crates/zeroclaw-runtime/src/cron/types.rs`) has **no `agent_alias` field**. The CLI handler (`src/cron/mod.rs`, `CronCommands::Update`) builds the patch with `..CronJobPatch::default()` and passes `agent_alias` only to `update_shell_job_with_approval`, where it names whose *risk profile validates a shell command* — it never reaches the stored row. So for prompt-only updates the flag is a pure no-op, reported as success.

We hit this operationally: attempted to reassign a weekly job to a different agent via the documented flag; CLI reported success; the job kept running under the old agent until the DB row was edited directly.

### Expected behavior

Either:
1. `cron update --agent <alias>` reassigns the job's executing agent (add `agent_alias` to `CronJobPatch`, persist it in `update_job`, emit a confirmation line naming the new agent), **or**
2. if reassignment is intentionally unsupported, the CLI rejects the flag with a clear error instead of reporting success.

Option 1 matches the flag's documented intent; option 2 is the minimal honest fix.

### Steps to reproduce

```bash
# 1. Create an agent cron job under agent A
zeroclaw cron add-agent '0 6 * * 1' 'do the weekly thing' --agent agent-a
# => created, id <id>

# 2. Reassign it to agent B
zeroclaw cron update <id> --agent agent-b
# => prints "updated", schedule, next run — looks successful

# 3. Check who actually owns it
zeroclaw cron list
# => agent_alias is still agent-a; the job ran (and will run) as agent-a
```

### Impact

Affected users: operators reassigning cron jobs between agents (e.g. moving a scheduled task to a secretary agent with different tools/skills).
Frequency: always — the update path has no field to carry the assignment.
Consequence: silent configuration drift; the operator believes a delegation took effect while the old agent keeps executing the job. In our case it required direct DB editing to recover.

### Logs / stack traces

No error is logged — the command exits 0 and prints the standard success block. Code references (v0.8.7, current master):

- `src/cron/mod.rs` — `CronCommands::Update` arm: `agent_alias` used only for `require_configured_agent` and `update_shell_job_with_approval(config, &agent_alias, &id, patch, false)`; the `CronJobPatch` literal uses `..CronJobPatch::default()`.
- `crates/zeroclaw-runtime/src/cron/types.rs` — `pub struct CronJobPatch` has no `agent_alias` field (the stored `CronJob.agent_alias` exists and is mutable only via direct DB writes).

### ZeroClaw version

v0.8.7 (reproduced on current master, commit 683d10139b)

### Rust version

rustc 1.97.1

### Operating system

Any — reproduced on Windows 11 (Windows Service install); the code path is platform-independent.

### Regression?

Unknown — the `CronJobPatch` struct appears to have never carried `agent_alias`, so this likely never worked, but we only discovered it now.

### Pre-flight checks

- [x] I reproduced this on the latest master branch or latest release.
- [x] I redacted secrets, tokens, and personal data from all submitted content.

issues.title: [Bug]: glob_search silently drops authorized matches outside the workspace, and rejects absolute patterns under read-only allowed roots
issues.body:
### Affected component

security/sandbox

### Severity

S2 - degraded behavior

### Current behavior

`glob_search` has two independent defects around `allowed_roots` that both make the tool misreport what it can see, in opposite directions:

1. **Silent discard of authorized matches outside the workspace** (`crates/zeroclaw-tools/src/glob_search.rs:140-142`). After a match passes the readability check (`is_resolved_path_readable`, which does consult `allowed_roots` and `allowed_roots_read_only`), the result is converted to a workspace-relative path with `resolved.strip_prefix(&workspace_canon)`. There is no `else` branch: if the resolved path is outside the workspace (reached through an explicit `allowed_roots` entry or a workspace symlink into one), `strip_prefix` returns `Err`, and the `if let Ok(rel) = ...` silently discards the match — no log, no counter, no indication to the caller that anything was dropped. The tool reports `success: true` and, if no other matches survive, `"No files matching pattern '<pattern>' found in workspace."` — even though the file exists and is explicitly authorized and readable.

2. **Absolute-pattern pre-check only sees the write-oriented tiers** (`glob_search.rs:64-66`). Before resolving anything, an absolute pattern is checked against `self.security.is_under_allowed_root(pattern)` (`crates/zeroclaw-config/src/policy.rs:4528-4535`), which only unions `allowed_roots` (read-write) and `allowed_roots_write_only`. It never consults `allowed_roots_read_only`. A sibling helper, `is_under_any_allowed_root` (`policy.rs:4546-4551`, doc comment: *"Union of all three root tiers; directionality is enforced later by the resolved-path checks"*), already exists and unions all three tiers but has no production caller for this check. The result: an absolute glob pattern under an explicit `allowed_roots_read_only` entry is rejected at this pre-check with `"Absolute paths are not allowed. Use a relative glob pattern."`, before ever reaching the resolved-path logic that would have allowed it — while the same pattern under a *write-only* root passes this pre-check (and then falls into bug 1 above).

Both bugs are reachable from the config a default install already has: `<install>/shared/skills` is pushed into `allowed_roots_read_only` for every agent, unconditionally, in `SecurityPolicy::for_agent` (`crates/zeroclaw-config/src/policy.rs:4772-4774`), and any `allowed_roots` entry (RW or RO) hits bug 1 once a match actually resolves outside the workspace.

The project's own `content_search` tool, which shares the same allowed-roots contract, does not have either defect: its output-line formatter, `relativize_path` (`content_search.rs:995-1004`, called at `:887`), falls back to the original absolute line when the workspace-relative `strip_prefix` fails, rather than discarding the match -- a separate include-glob filter, `internal_include_matches` (`content_search.rs:680`), independently makes the same fall-back choice when a path is outside the workspace, though that one is a filter predicate, not the result formatter. `content_search` also has no raw-string pre-check ahead of the resolved-path gate (`content_search.rs:196-198`).

### Expected behavior

`docs/book/src/security/autonomy.md:79-80` states the contract: *"`workspace_only = true` restricts reads and writes to `<workspace>/**`, plus any configured `allowed_roots` for the requested access mode."* For a read tool like `glob_search`, "the requested access mode" should include files reachable through `allowed_roots` (RW) and `allowed_roots_read_only` alike, consistent with what `is_resolved_path_readable` already grants.

Two ways to close the gap, left to the maintainer to pick. Both are defects under the code and docs as they stand today. For context: in a now-`DISMISSED` review on PR #10308 (2026-08-28), a contributor wrote that `glob_search` "explicitly promises workspace-only discovery and workspace-relative results, so its inability to enumerate this external root is a documented capability limit rather than a second reason to refuse the patch" — which does track a real artifact, the tool's own description string (`glob_search.rs:27-28`: *"Search for files matching a glob pattern within the workspace. Returns a sorted list of matching file paths relative to the workspace root."*). That comment addressed whether `glob_search` can enumerate an external root *at all*; it does not address the asymmetry reported here, where RW and write-only roots already pass the pre-check (and then silently lose their results) while only read-only roots are rejected outright. Whatever the intended scope, today's behavior is neither "workspace-only" nor "all allowed_roots, consistently":

- **Option A — honor the full contract:** replace the raw-pattern pre-check with `is_under_any_allowed_root` (or drop it and rely solely on the resolved-path gate, matching `content_search`), and give the formatting step a fallback for paths outside the workspace (e.g. `unwrap_or(&resolved)`, matching `content_search.rs:680`) so an authorized external match is reported with an absolute (or allowed-root-relative) path instead of being dropped.
- **Option B — make "workspace-only" tool explicit:** if `glob_search` is intentionally scoped to the workspace regardless of `allowed_roots`, reject *every* absolute/external pattern (RW, write-only, and read-only alike) with a truthful message, instead of the current behavior, which admits RW and write-only patterns at the pre-check and only then drops their results silently.

Either option removes the current situation, where the tool's behavior depends on which of the three root tiers is configured, without that distinction being visible to the caller or documented anywhere.

### Steps to reproduce

```bash
Prerequisites: a checkout of zeroclaw at or after 5d4b18d335780af8bf15979b2f45e541f91c5eb9
(any commit where crates/zeroclaw-tools/src/glob_search.rs matches the version quoted above).

Case 1 - silent discard of an authorized external match:
1. Configure an agent with:
   - workspace = <workspace>
   - allowed_roots = ["<outside>"]  # read-write tier
2. Put a readable file at <outside>/allowed.txt.
3. From inside the agent's workspace, create a symlink `link -> <outside>`
   (or, on a host where <outside> is reachable without a symlink, skip this step).
4. Ask the agent (or call the tool directly) with:
   glob_search(pattern = "link/*.txt")
5. Expected: the response lists allowed.txt (it is explicitly authorized and readable).
   Observed: success: true, output "No files matching pattern 'link/*.txt' found in
   workspace." -- the file is silently dropped by strip_prefix at glob_search.rs:140.

Case 2 - absolute pattern rejected under a read-only allowed root:
1. Configure an agent with:
   - workspace = <workspace>
   - allowed_roots_read_only = ["<ro_root>"]
2. Put a readable file at <ro_root>/shared.txt.
3. Call: glob_search(pattern = "<ro_root>/*.txt")   # absolute pattern
4. Expected: the response lists shared.txt (is_resolved_path_readable already grants it).
   Observed: success: false, error "Absolute paths are not allowed. Use a relative glob
   pattern." -- rejected at the pre-check (glob_search.rs:64-66) before resolution, because
   is_under_allowed_root does not see allowed_roots_read_only.

Minimal regression tests (predictions written before running; run against
5d4b18d335780af8bf15979b2f45e541f91c5eb9 on WSL/Ubuntu 24.04,
cargo test -p zeroclaw-tools --lib glob_search:: -- --test-threads=1
-- confirmed: both fail exactly as predicted; 15/15 other glob_search tests unaffected):

- glob_search_drops_authorized_match_outside_workspace -- Case 1, via a workspace symlink into
  an RW allowed_roots entry (Unix-only, std::os::unix::fs::symlink). Panic: "allowed.txt
  sits under an explicit allowed_roots entry and must be listed, not silently dropped by
  strip_prefix; got: No files matching pattern 'link/*.txt' found in workspace."
- glob_search_rejects_absolute_pattern_under_read_only_root -- Case 2, with a literal
  /-prefixed absolute pattern (also Unix-only: on Windows a C:\... pattern does not start with
  / or \\ and bypasses the pre-check entirely). Panic: "an absolute pattern under an explicit
  allowed_roots_read_only entry must not be rejected before resolution; got error:
  Some(\"Absolute paths are not allowed. Use a relative glob pattern.\")"

Full result: test result: FAILED. 15 passed; 2 failed -- only the two new tests fail; every
pre-existing glob_search test (including the sibling write-only-root symlink test) still
passes, so the failures isolate the two reported mechanisms and nothing else.
```

### Impact

```
Affected users: any agent with allowed_roots (RW), allowed_roots_read_only, or a cross-agent
  read/write grant outside its own workspace, using glob_search with an absolute pattern or a
  symlink into an allowed root. allowed_roots_read_only is not a rare configuration: every
  install's default <install>/shared/skills root is pushed into it unconditionally
  (policy.rs:4772-4774).
Frequency: always, for the two reproductions above; not conditional on race or timing.
Consequence: glob_search misreports what the agent can see in both directions -- it can claim
  "no files found" for files that are explicitly authorized and readable (case 1), or refuse an
  absolute pattern as categorically disallowed when it is explicitly readable (case 2). An agent
  or operator relying on the tool's report to decide whether a resource exists gets a false
  negative. Observed in practice: an agent looped re-deliberating after trusting a false "no
  files matching" response.
```

### Logs / stack traces

```
---- glob_search::tests::glob_search_drops_authorized_match_outside_workspace stdout ----

thread 'glob_search::tests::glob_search_drops_authorized_match_outside_workspace' panicked at
crates/zeroclaw-tools/src/glob_search.rs:443:9:
allowed.txt sits under an explicit allowed_roots entry and must be listed, not silently dropped
by strip_prefix; got: No files matching pattern 'link/*.txt' found in workspace.
note: run with `RUST_BACKTRACE=1` environment variable to display a backtrace

---- glob_search::tests::glob_search_rejects_absolute_pattern_under_read_only_root stdout ----

thread 'glob_search::tests::glob_search_rejects_absolute_pattern_under_read_only_root' panicked at
crates/zeroclaw-tools/src/glob_search.rs:480:9:
an absolute pattern under an explicit allowed_roots_read_only entry must not be rejected before
resolution; got error: Some("Absolute paths are not allowed. Use a relative glob pattern.")

test result: FAILED. 15 passed; 2 failed; 0 ignored; 0 measured; 1366 filtered out
```

### ZeroClaw version

5d4b18d335780af8bf15979b2f45e541f91c5eb9 (origin/master)

### Rust version

_No response_

### Operating system

Reproduced on Ubuntu 24.04 (WSL2); both defects are OS-independent in the code path that matters for Case 1 and Case 2 as written. Note: the absolute-pattern pre-check itself is not reached the same way on Windows for a native `C:\...` pattern -- it bypasses this specific pre-check and falls into bug 1's path instead -- but that does not change the two mechanisms reported here, both of which are reproduced on Linux/macOS as written.

### Regression?

issues.title: [Bug]: glob_search never lists files under allowed roots outside the workspace
issues.body:
### Summary

`glob_search` never lists files outside the agent workspace, even when the pattern is an absolute path under an allowed root. The pre-check accepts the pattern (since #3434, which closed #3082), but every match is then dropped when it is converted to a workspace-relative path, so the tool always answers "No files matching pattern … found in workspace". Read-only roots granted through `workspace.access` are also refused at the pre-check.

`file_read` and `content_search` already handle the same paths correctly, so an agent can read and grep files under an allowed root but cannot list them.

### Affected component

Tools (`crates/zeroclaw-tools/src/glob_search.rs`)

### Current behavior

1. Absolute pattern under a read-write `allowed_roots` entry: accepted, then every result outside the workspace is discarded by `resolved.strip_prefix(&workspace_canon)`; output is "No files matching pattern … found in workspace".
2. Absolute pattern under a read-only root (from `workspace.access = { other = "read" }`): rejected with "Absolute paths are not allowed. Use a relative glob pattern.", because the pre-check uses `is_under_allowed_root` (read-write + write-only) instead of a readable-roots check.

### Expected behavior

Absolute patterns under any readable root (read-write or read-only) are accepted, and matches outside the workspace are returned with their absolute path, as `content_search` does. Per-file readability checks stay as they are, so write-only roots never surface.

### Steps to reproduce

```toml
[risk_profiles.p]
level = "supervised"
auto_approve = ["glob_search", "file_read"]
allowed_roots = ["/srv/project"]          # contains docs/offer.md

[agents.a]
risk_profile = "p"
workspace = { path = "/srv/project/.agent" }
```

Ask the agent to run `glob_search` with pattern `/srv/project/docs/*.md` → "No files matching pattern …". `file_read` on `/srv/project/docs/offer.md` succeeds.

### Impact

Any agent whose documents live outside its workspace (workspace for identity and memory, documents reached through `allowed_roots` or `workspace.access`) cannot discover files and falls back to guessing paths. Found while running one agent per project folder with the agent files in a subfolder.

### ZeroClaw version

master 683d10139 (0.8.7)

### Regression?

No: the result filter has been workspace-only since before #3434; the pre-check change in #3434 made the pattern acceptable without making the results reachable.

issues.body:
After a browser login, the gateway shows the token on a page to anyone who arrives with the right one-time codes in the URL. Nothing checks that the person seeing the page is the one who started the login, so an attacker can log in as themselves and then trick a victim into opening that final page. The victim copies what they think is their own token, but it is the attacker's, so everything the victim does afterwards is saved under the attacker's account where the attacker can read it.

### Affected component

gateway/api

### Severity

S0 - data loss / security risk

### Current behavior

`GET /oidc/callback` (`crates/zeroclaw-gateway/src/api_oidc.rs:704-794`) consumes the flow for the given `state`, exchanges the code, and renders the access token in `success_page` (lines 668-702). Nothing ties the browser that completes the flow to the browser that started it. On the PR #11965 head the same page remains for enrollment-mode flows and is still unbound.

### Expected behavior

The callback should finish a flow only in the browser that started it, for example with the short-lived binding cookie PR #11965 adds for dashboard sign-in. A callback without the binding should be refused and the flow consumed. If the token-display page is kept for zerocode or web clients, it should carry the same binding.

### Steps to reproduce

```text
1. In the attacker's browser start GET /oidc/login/<alias>, log in at the identity provider as
   the attacker, and capture the final redirect URL (/oidc/callback?code=..&state=..) before
   the browser follows it.
2. Send that URL to a victim, who opens it in their own browser.
3. The victim sees a "Signed in" page with a token; if they paste it into their client, every
   action is attributed to the attacker's principal.
Source-traced at master 5d4b18d335; not executed.
```

### Impact

Everything the victim does with the pasted token is attributed to the attacker's principal, and the victim's sessions and private memory land where the attacker can read them. The page is a manual-copy fallback today, so the likelihood is low, but PR #11965 documents it as the handoff for clients other than the dashboard. Related tracker #8289.

### Logs / stack traces

_No response_

### ZeroClaw version

master 5d4b18d335 (v0.8.7)

### Rust version

n/a (source review); CI pins 1.98.0

### Operating system

Any; reviewed in source on macOS

### Regression?

No, first-time setup

### Pre-flight checks

- [ ] I reproduced this on the latest master branch or latest release.
Source-traced at master 5d4b18d335; no runtime reproduction was run.
- [X] I redacted secrets, tokens, and personal data from all submitted content.

### Recommended action

Reuse PR #11965's per-flow binding cookie for the enrollment mode of `/oidc/callback` so only the starting browser can finish it. Refuse and consume the flow when the binding is missing, and cover both outcomes with tests. If no client still needs the token-display page once the dashboard consumes sessions, remove it.

issues.body:
### Current status — 2026-09-28

**Still open; #10412 is a partial implementation.** #10412 extracts the shared atomic session-ownership claim and removes one stale-admin exception. Its stated scope leaves other stale-grant paths in this issue unresolved. Landing that PR alone must not be treated as full issue completion.

The remaining acceptance is still the queued-operation/current-authority behavior described below. #11197 remains a separate resume/environment follow-up. The issue should close only after the complete acceptance is implemented and verified.

---

### Affected component

security/sandbox

### Severity

S0 - data loss / security risk

### Current behavior

Source review of the landed #10265 commit found that queued session operations can retain an administrator's ownership bypass after that administrator is demoted. I have not executed a runtime reproduction.

The caller must initially be a named local administrator, target another principal's session, and lose administrator status while waiting for admission. Ordinary method and target-agent/root permissions remain. The live target session need not change.

[`scoped_principal_id`](https://github.com/zeroclaw-labs/zeroclaw/blob/73e2a4a15ddbdb01ffb4a044dc6c5c8dd7835110/crates/zeroclaw-runtime/src/rpc/dispatch.rs#L1841-L1847) derives the ownership bypass from the connection's stamped `self.auth.grants.admin`. [`recheck_authority_after_admission`](https://github.com/zeroclaw-labs/zeroclaw/blob/73e2a4a15ddbdb01ffb4a044dc6c5c8dd7835110/crates/zeroclaw-runtime/src/rpc/dispatch.rs#L1280-L1318) returns fresh grants without updating that stamp. In the prompt path, ownership is revalidated before this refresh, and the later agent/root/tool checks do not repeat the owner decision.

Close, kill, and delete also revalidate after admission without refreshing authority. In particular, [delete chooses between owner-predicated and unpredicated storage deletion](https://github.com/zeroclaw-labs/zeroclaw/blob/73e2a4a15ddbdb01ffb4a044dc6c5c8dd7835110/crates/zeroclaw-runtime/src/rpc/dispatch.rs#L5933-L5990) using the stale administrator scope. The demoted caller can therefore still delete another principal's durable session.

This is a post-merge repair for #10265 under the current-authority and session-ownership contracts in #7141 and #8290.

### Expected behavior

Resolve current authority and derive the owner scope together after admission, before any post-wait effect. Apply this consistently to prompt, destructive operations, and queued resume paths. Removing administrator status must remove cross-principal access even if ordinary method and agent/root permissions remain.

A focused admission test should demote a queued administrator, verify denial against a foreign-owned session without modifying its durable data, and retain an own-session positive control. Cover the destructive path as well as prompt if they use separate authorization logic.

### Steps to reproduce

```bash
# Source-derived regression scenario; not executed.
# 1. Create a live session owned by zeroclaw_user.
# 2. Connect zeroclaw_operator as a named local administrator.
# 3. Hold the session's admission permit and queue a foreign-session delete.
# 4. Remove administrator status while retaining the ordinary delete method
#    permission and applicable target-agent/root grants.
# 5. Release admission without replacing the target's live incarnation.
# Expected: deny the foreign-owner operation and preserve durable data.
# Source path: the stamped admin bypass selects unpredicated deletion.
# Positive control: a permitted operation on the caller's own session succeeds.
```

### Impact

Deployments that use named principals, live grant changes, and queued session operations can retain revoked cross-principal privileges. The destructive variant risks another principal's session data. This is not a claim that an ordinary never-administrator caller can acquire admin privileges.

### Logs / stack traces

```text
No runtime logs captured. Evidence is the linked source at the landed commit.
```

### ZeroClaw version

`73e2a4a15ddbdb01ffb4a044dc6c5c8dd7835110` (landed #10265).

### Rust version

Not built locally for this report; source inspection only.

### Operating system

No runtime reproduction on a specific OS. The identified authorization path is platform-independent Rust code.

### Regression?

Unknown

The defect is in the newly landed principal-ownership boundary; no before/after runtime comparison was performed.

### Pre-flight checks

- [ ] I reproduced this on the latest master branch or latest release.
- [x] I redacted secrets, tokens, and personal data from all submitted content.

The reproduction checkbox is intentionally unchecked because this is a source-review finding.

issues.body:
### Summary

Let an account that signs in to the dashboard with OIDC, without administrator rights, chat with the agents its grants allow, as itself.

### Problem statement

**Dashboard sign-in (#11961) gives non-administrator accounts the dashboard, but not its chat.** The chat runs in the gateway's own process with the shared operator's authority. Offering it as it is would let a scoped account act with the operator's grants, and see conversations that aren't its own. So today the chat is administrator-only. An account that is allowed to use an agent from zerocode can't use that agent from the dashboard.

### Proposed solution

**Serve a scoped account's chat through the daemon's session methods**, on a daemon connection that presents that account's own token. The daemon then runs the conversation as that principal, under its grants, and keeps it as that principal's own.

- **One conversation per chat socket.**
  - It is created when the socket opens. It is closed, never deleted, when the socket closes, at sign-out, shortly before the token expires, when the account loses access, and at a daemon reload.
  - No other socket reopens it, so nothing about a conversation is shared between sockets.
- **Limits:** at most four chats per sign-in and 32 per account. A conversation still being created, or not yet closed, counts. A chat past a limit is told so and closed.
- **The token goes only to the provider that issued it.** Each chat connection is bound to the sign-in's identity provider, so a provider repointed since then never receives the token.
- **Unchanged:** administrators keep today's chat and its history. Paired browsers and installs without dashboard sign-in are unchanged too.

### Non-goals / out of scope

- **History across sockets.** A scoped conversation ends with its socket; restoring a non-live conversation to its owner is #11737.
- Image upload and model switching for scoped accounts.
- Any change to the daemon's session ownership rules.
- Splitting the gateway out of the daemon.
- Identity providers that dashboard sign-in can't use yet (a private CA, extra scopes, resource indicators).

### Alternatives considered

- **One shared daemon connection per sign-in, with the gateway mapping dashboard ids to conversations.** This was tried. It needs cross-socket state, reattachment and cleanup logic that is hard to keep consistent with the daemon on every failure path.
- **Keeping the chat administrator-only:** the status quo.

### Acceptance criteria

- A scoped account chats with an agent it is granted. The daemon runs the turn as that account, under its grants, and nobody else's dashboard lists the conversation.
- Another account cannot read, rename, delete, close, stop or answer approvals for that conversation, even knowing its live id.
- Reloading the page or closing the tab ends the conversation; the next message starts a new one.
- A fifth chat in one sign-in is refused without closing the other four. Signing out and in again frees no slot until the conversations are closed.
- Sign-out, token expiry, revocation and a daemon reload close the account's conversations. The transcripts are kept.
- A provider repointed after sign-in never receives the account's token.
- Administrators, paired browsers and installs without sign-in behave as before.

### Architecture impact

- The daemon gains a provider-bound in-process connection, which needs a runtime placement row: proposed in #11963.
- It builds on the in-process RPC client (#11186), the daemon's retirement of orphaned remote sessions (#11964) and dashboard sign-in (#11965).
- The wire protocol is unchanged.

### Risk and rollback

- **Off by default:** it applies only when dashboard sign-in is configured.
- **To roll back,** revert the change, or remove the providers from `[gateway.dashboard_sign_in]`, which also closes every dashboard session.
- **Risk** is concentrated in isolation between accounts and in cleanup when a socket or session ends. Both are covered by tests that attack with real conversation ids.

### Expected routing

Should attach to an existing roadmap/tracker issue

### Next decision surface

Milestone v0.9.0, as the second half of dashboard sign-in (#11961, under #8289). The v0.9.0 tracker #7432 gives scoped dashboard chat a November 3 go/no-go; if it misses, sign-in ships without it.

### Breaking change?

No

### Data hygiene checks

- [X] I removed personal/sensitive data from examples, payloads, and logs.
- [X] I used neutral, project-focused wording and placeholders.

issues.body:
Found while auditing the host this project builds against. Every cited line was opened and every quote checked against HEAD before filing.

**Location.** `crates/zeroclaw-config/src/schema.rs:6980-7025`; `crates/zeroclaw-config/fixtures/v1.toml:511-516`; `pairing.rs:8-10`, `:126`, `:284-286`; `api_pairing.rs:303-368`.

**Code.** The reference fixture ships all five keys:

```toml
[gateway.pairing_dashboard]
code_length = 8
code_ttl_secs = 3600
max_pending_codes = 3
max_failed_attempts = 5
lockout_secs = 300
```

The guard uses hardcoded constants instead:

```rust
const MAX_PAIR_ATTEMPTS: u32 = 5;
const PAIR_LOCKOUT_SECS: u64 = 300; // 5 minutes
```

```rust
/// Generate a 6-digit numeric pairing code ...
fn generate_code() -> String { const UPPER_BOUND: u32 = 1_000_000;
```

**Failure path.** A repository-wide search confines `code_length`, `code_ttl_secs`, `max_pending_codes`, `max_failed_attempts`, and the `pairing_dashboard` field itself to `schema.rs` and the fixture. The production construction at `zeroclaw-gateway/src/lib.rs:1228` passes only `require_pairing` and `paired_tokens`; `PairingGuard::new` takes no config, and `zeroclaw-runtime/src/security/pairing.rs` is a one-line re-export of the same type, so there is no second implementation that reads it. Hardening a reachable pairing endpoint is therefore void: codes stay 6 digits while the config's own default claims 8, which is itself evidence the wiring never existed, and lockout stays at 5 attempts per 300 seconds. Because `code_ttl_secs` is unread and `PairingStore` exposes only `pending_count()` with no push or insert, `PendingPairing.expires_at` is dead code and `initiate_pairing` records no expiry, so `pairing_code` is a bare `Option<String>` cleared only on consumption. Setting `code_ttl_secs = 60` still leaves a code that is valid indefinitely, sitting in console output and logs. Both endpoints are routed (`lib.rs:1615-1616`, `:1858-1859`), which is what makes this reachable rather than theoretical, and it compounds F2 directly.

**Fix.** Pass the config into `PairingGuard::new` and read all five keys, or delete the section from the schema and the fixture. Independently of that decision, give the pending code a timestamp and reject it past its TTL.

---

Happy to open a PR if you want one; say which direction you prefer and I will follow the shape you name rather than guessing.

issues.body:
### Affected component

memory

### Severity

S0 - data loss / security risk

### Current behavior

A principal-bound ("owned") session is meant to keep all memory reads and writes on its owner's private plane. Two tool paths still build or hold memory handles that were never scoped to the owner, so an owned session can reach the agent's **shared** plane through them. Both were named as out-of-scope residual gaps in #11225, which fixes the `delegate` path only.

1. **`spawn_subagent`** — `child_run_overrides` sets `memory: None` (`crates/zeroclaw-runtime/src/tools/spawn_subagent.rs:68-71`). With no memory override, `agent::run` builds the child's memory with an unscoped `zeroclaw_memory::create_memory_for_agent(&config, agent_alias, None)` (`crates/zeroclaw-runtime/src/agent/loop_.rs:1472`). The SubAgent of an owned session therefore reads and writes the agent's shared plane. The tool is kept for administrators and principals with wildcard agent selectors, and a delegated child can reach it when its policy admits it.

2. **`execute_pipeline`** (opt-in: `[pipeline] enabled` with a memory tool in `pipeline.allowed_tools`; off by default) — `PipelineTool` stores its own `tools: Vec<Arc<dyn Tool>>` captured at construction (`crates/zeroclaw-tools/src/pipeline.rs:69-80`). Session owner routing replaces memory tools in the registry via `rebind_memory_tools` (`crates/zeroclaw-runtime/src/tools/scoped.rs:97`, called from `agent/agent.rs:1993`), which does not reach handles the pipeline already holds.

Both contradict the session-pinning contract that owned sessions stay on their owner's private plane.

### Expected behavior

Every memory handle reachable from an owned session — including a `spawn_subagent` child and any tool a pipeline invokes — is built from the owning principal's scope. Where the owner cannot be carried, the call is refused rather than falling back to the shared plane.

### Steps to reproduce

```bash
# Source-traced from master 0a2dae1837; not executed.
# Path 1: spawn_subagent
#   1. Owned RPC session for principal P on agent A; A's risk profile allows spawn_subagent.
#   2. P's session calls spawn_subagent with a prompt that runs memory_store "P-MARKER".
#   3. child_run_overrides passes memory: None; agent::run builds unscoped agent memory.
#   4. Expected P-MARKER on P's private plane for A; it lands on A's shared plane.
# Path 2: execute_pipeline
#   1. [pipeline] enabled = true with memory_store in pipeline.allowed_tools.
#   2. Owned session for P runs execute_pipeline with a memory_store step.
#   3. PipelineTool invokes its captured pre-routing memory_store handle.
#   4. The write lands on the shared plane rather than P's private plane.
```

### Impact

Cross-principal memory isolation for owned sessions does not hold across the full tool surface: a principal's writes can land where other principals using the same agent can read them, and a child can read shared rows the owner's session is meant to be isolated from. The private-plane feature is on master only (not in a release; latest is v0.8.5), so there is no deployed exposure yet — this should be closed before v0.9.0 ships multi-user sessions.

Related: #11225 (fixes the `delegate` path; also has three open FATAL findings on skill aliases and background result retrieval), #11198, tracker #8290. Separately, the Permission inheritance section of `docs/book/src/agents/delegation.md` lists six inheritance axes and none of them is the principal; that doctrine change is being drafted on its own and is not this issue's scope.

labels.name: bug
labels.description: Something isn't working

issues.body:
### Affected component

runtime/daemon

### Severity

S2 - degraded behavior

### Current behavior

## Summary

The top-level agent uses native tool calling correctly on every iteration. When it delegates to another agent (same provider profile, `mode = "independent"`), the delegate's reply comes back as the model's **raw text tool-call syntax**, which is never parsed or executed:

```
[Agent 'gamma' (custom.lemonade/LFM2.5-24B-A2B-GGUF)]
<|tool_call_start|>[file_read(path='/root/zc-repro/data/estado.txt')]<|tool_call_end|>
```

This is the model's own chat-template tool-call format (LFM2.5). The model typically emits it when the request has **no `tools` array** and the tools are only described in the prompt. That suggests the delegate's request is built without native tools, or that its response is not run through the tool-call parser.

We saw the same behaviour in an earlier test (2026-10-31) with `mode = "bounded"`, so it does not look mode-specific. We have not re-run `bounded` with this exact config.

## Minimal config

```toml
schema_version = 3

[providers.models.custom.lemonade]
uri = "http://<host>:13305/api/v1"
model = "LFM2.5-24B-A2B-GGUF"
api_key = "none"
wire_api = "chat_completions"
native_tools = true

[runtime_profiles.repro]
max_delegation_depth = 3
max_tool_iterations = 8

[risk_profiles.repro]
level = "supervised"
allowed_tools = ["delegate", "file_read"]
auto_approve = ["delegate", "file_read"]
always_ask = []
workspace_only = true

[risk_profiles.repro.delegation_policy]
mode = "allow"

[agents.alpha]
model_provider = "custom.lemonade"
risk_profile = "repro"
runtime_profile = "repro"
delegates = [{ agent = "beta", mode = "independent" }]
[agents.alpha.workspace]
path = "ws/alpha"

[agents.beta]
model_provider = "custom.lemonade"
risk_profile = "repro"
runtime_profile = "repro"
delegates = [{ agent = "gamma", mode = "independent" }]
[agents.beta.workspace]
path = "ws/beta"

[agents.gamma]
model_provider = "custom.lemonade"
risk_profile = "repro"
runtime_profile = "repro"
[agents.gamma.workspace]
path = "ws/gamma"
```

`ws/gamma/estado.txt` contains a marker string.

## Observed (`data/state/runtime-trace.jsonl`)

- **Every top-level iteration uses native tools:** `llm_request` has `tools_count: 2`, and `llm_response` has `native_tool_calls: 1, parsed_tool_calls: 1`.
- **Iteration 2:** a `delegate` call (`agent: "gamma"`) succeeds after 5 s. Its `tool_call_result.output` is the raw text tool call shown above.
- **No delegate trace:** there are no `llm_request` / `llm_response` events for the delegate's own model call, so we cannot see whether its request carried `tools`.
- **End of run:** the parent then tries `file_read` itself, gets path errors (see the note below), and ends with `tool_loop_exhausted (LocalIterations(8))`.

### Expected behavior

- The delegate uses the same provider profile, including `native_tools = true`, and returns a parsed tool call that is executed in its own loop, followed by its final answer.
- Alternatively, if a delegate cannot use native tools, ZeroClaw parses its text-mode output with the same recovery the top-level loop has.

The delegate's LLM calls should also appear in the runtime trace, attributed to the delegate alias.

### Steps to reproduce

```bash
zeroclaw --config-dir ./zc-repro agent --agent alpha -m "Delega en beta esta tarea: beta debe delegar en gamma para que gamma lea el fichero estado.txt de su workspace con la herramienta file_read y devuelva su contenido literal. Responde solo con el contenido."
```

prs.title: fix(rpc): hold current authority through session effects
prs.body:
## Summary

- **Base branch:** `master`
- **What changed and why:** #11234 made queued session operations recheck the caller's authority after they wait. Several session effects still committed after another await, or never rechecked at all, so a revocation, demotion or ownership change that landed in between still let them through. This finishes those effects:
  - `session/configure` commits its overrides and provider in one step, under the caller's authority lease, rather than in two awaited writes after the recheck.
  - `session/append` and `session/rename` decide under the store's write lock, by the row's current owner and the caller's current authority. Append seeds the live Agent and sends its event inside the same commit.
  - For a remote client, configure, append, rename, abort and steering also check that the caller's TUI still owns the session when they commit. A same-generation resume by another TUI used to leave the old TUI able to reconfigure, write, cancel and steer. Steering it had already queued is now revoked when the session changes hands.
  - `session/abort` decides under the incarnation and cancellation locks with the caller's authority lease.
  - `session/run-once` looks up its id under current authority and requires `sessions:update`, since it closes the session it creates. If the close is refused after the turn, the call returns that error instead of reporting success. A remote caller can now name its own id, and the call keeps the generation it published even if that session is removed before it returns.
- **Scope boundary:** No new RPC method, config key or persisted schema. The SOP read repairs from #11411 are a separate follow-up after #12232 (which replaced #11220). Principal-owned Chat restore after a restart is #11737. Prompt admission, `session/new` resume and the destructive operations #11234 already covers are unchanged.
- **Blast radius:** RPC session handlers in `zeroclaw-runtime` (`rpc/dispatch.rs`, `rpc/session.rs`, the run-once doc in `rpc/types.rs`) and two new default methods on `SessionBackend` in `zeroclaw-infra`, implemented for SQLite and for JSONL append. Gateway and channel sessions are not touched, since append still refuses any session that RPC does not write.
- **Linked issue(s):** Closes #11126. Related #11234, #11408, #11411.

### What this does, simply

When an RPC client asks to change a session, the daemon checks the caller is allowed and then makes the change. Between those two steps it often has to wait: for the session's queue, a lock or the database. #11234 added a second check after those waits. A few changes still did more waiting after that second check, or skipped it. So a caller whose access was taken away at the wrong moment could still add a message, rename a session, change its model, cancel its turn or steer it.

This PR moves the final check to the moment the change is written, and holds it there until the write is done. It also covers a remote case: the TUI that loses a session to another TUI can no longer act on it, and any steering it had already queued is dropped.

## Testing (required)

### How you can test (when useful)

- **Reviewer testing requested?** N/A: each case is a timing window that the focused tests open with test pauses. A manual run cannot hit them reliably.

### How I tested

On Linux x86_64 (Rust 1.98.0), at ffcfe904b3 (tree 3650786e3e), on master 72167d12e2:

- **CI checks relied on and why they cover this change:** the Rust lint and test jobs build and run `zeroclaw-infra` and `zeroclaw-runtime`, where all the changes are.
- **Known CI coverage gap, if any:** none for this change; the windows are covered by the focused tests below.
- **Commands run and tail output:**
  - `cargo fetch --locked`, `cargo fmt --all -- --check`, the comment-hygiene gate and `git diff --check` against master: clean.
  - `cargo check --locked --workspace --exclude zeroclaw-desktop --all-targets`: clean.
  - `cargo clippy --locked -p zeroclaw-infra -p zeroclaw-runtime --all-targets -- -D warnings`: clean.
  - `cargo test -p zeroclaw-infra --lib`: `test result: ok. 329 passed; 0 failed`.
  - `cargo test -p zeroclaw-runtime --lib`: `test result: ok. 6084 passed; 0 failed; 10 ignored`.
  - The ported tests three runs in a row at 4ad6aebb42: runtime `12 passed; 0 failed` and infra `2 passed; 0 failed`, each time. At ffcfe904b3, the configure and remote session tests three runs in a row: `165 passed; 0 failed` each time.
- **Beyond CI, what did you manually verify?** I undid one functional line at a time (19 changes) and ran the session tests for each. Fifteen failed the tests written for them:
  - the configure commit without its authority check;
  - the SQLite append, SQLite rename or JSONL append without theirs;
  - configure, append, rename or abort without the TUI fence;
  - abort without its authority lease;
  - a create-only `session/new` capturing access, or re-reading its generation;
  - steering ignoring a revoked TUI binding, or a rebind that keeps the old binding;
  - run-once without the `sessions:update` check, or hiding a refused close.

  Four fail nothing, and I couldn't make them observable:
  - **Configure leaving automatic routing on after an explicit model choice:** the flag has no accessor outside the agent, the same gap master has.
  - **Run-once looking up its id by the connection's stamped scope:** the ownership check and the create-only `session/new` that follow refuse the same cases.
  - **Steering's TUI fence at enqueue:** steering admission fences the same TUI just before, and the revoked binding drops the steer when the turn consumes it.
  - **Steering resolving its grants without holding the lease:** only a publication racing that one read would show it.
- **Visual interface evidence:** N/A
- **Tested revision, interface, and evidence path:** ffcfe904b3, RPC handlers through their unit-test dispatchers.
- **Screenshot or exact-output evidence:** N/A
- **Action or changed state and observed result:** N/A
- **If any command was intentionally skipped, why:** No live daemon, macOS or Windows run, and no full workspace test suite. The infra and runtime libraries cover the changed code.

## Security & Privacy Impact (required)

- New permissions, capabilities, or file system access scope? No. `session/run-once` now requires `sessions:update` as well, which only narrows who can call it.
- New external network calls? No
- Secrets / tokens / credentials handling changed? No
- PII, real identities, or personal data in diff, tests, fixtures, or docs? No
- Prompt injection or untrusted model-visible text introduced/changed? No. Steering that a TUI queued before it lost the session is now dropped before the model sees it.
- If any `Yes`, describe the risk and mitigation: N/A

## Compatibility (required)

- Backward compatible? No, in three narrow cases:
  - A principal granted `sessions:create` and `sessions:execute` but not `sessions:update` can no longer use `session/run-once`.
  - On a JSONL session backend, `session/rename` now returns an error instead of succeeding without storing the name. Guarded appends work on both backends.
  - A remote TUI that lost a session to another TUI now gets `SESSION_NOT_OWNED` for append, rename, abort and steer on that session.
- Config / env / CLI surface changed? No
- Rust/MSRV/toolchain floor changed? No
- Upgrade steps: grant `sessions:update` to any permission profile that uses `session/run-once`. Nothing else needs to change.

## Rollback (required for medium/high-risk PRs)

- **Fast rollback command/path:** `git revert` the merge commit. The guarded writes add no state, so nothing needs migrating back.
- **Feature flags or config toggles:** None
- **Observable failure symptoms:** RPC clients getting `FORBIDDEN`, `AUTH_REQUIRED` or `SESSION_NOT_OWNED` on append, rename, abort, steer or configure without any policy or ownership change; run-once returning "Turn completed, but could not close transient session".

## Supersede Attribution (required only when `Supersedes #` is used)

Not used. #11408 and #11411 stay open for their SOP parts. The session-effect commits here are Aarlington's work, kept as cherry-picks where they applied and otherwise ported with a `Co-authored-by` trailer:

- **Configure:**
  - f455ba115b and aaa681d085 (#11411), cherry-picked.
  - A follow-up keeps master's explicit-model routing step from #11516 in the atomic commit and removes the setter it replaced.
  - 3a833e4cdd and 561ece3f0e, ported onto master's version of their test.
- **Run-once lookup:** 85567e108c, cherry-picked.
- **Operator abort test:** 75a72e84a4, cherry-picked.
- **Append and rename:** the guarded writes from #11408's master merge 90a5978dbb, with the tests from 874b4e43bc and f00fe86148.
- **Remote ownership:** b86d4536bb, ported. Abort now uses `signal_cancellation_authorized`, and `abort_session_for_generation` is removed because nothing calls it anymore.
- **Steering:** 9c7cfd9823, and the steering part of 874b4e43bc.
- **Create-only generation:** the rest of 874b4e43bc.
- **Run-once cleanup:** 569e6fc11d, with the test changes from 08033c25a4 and 2e6c2b7835.
- **Abort test:** one new test of my own. Abort no longer rechecks before cancelling, so nothing else covered the handler passing its authority lease into `signal_cancellation_authorized`.
- **Not carried:**
  - 70a39b766f and ebfa6a1874: master's tests already publish config through the commit API.
  - The `sop_principal.rs` part of 70a39b766f goes with the SOP-reads follow-up.

IftekharUddin found that configure still committed without checking the current TUI owner and wrote the fix and its test: 66a93d5446, cherry-picked as ffcfe904b3 with IftekharUddin as author.

prs.title: feat(channels): add one-tap Matrix approval reactions
prs.body:
## Summary

- **Base branch:** `master`
- **What changed and why:**
  - Matrix approval prompts now arrive with ✅, 🔁 and ❌ reactions seeded by the bot. An authorized operator taps ✅ to approve the call once, 🔁 to approve it and allow the tool for the rest of the session (the typed `always`), or ❌ to deny it. Today the operator has to copy the 8-character token and type `<TOKEN> approve`, which is awkward on mobile clients.
  - The design follows the Mattermost one-tap approvals from #10358: the same ✅/❌ pair, the bot's own reactions ignored, and reaction decisions refused while the bot's identity is unknown. Mattermost leaves `always` typed-only. Matrix adds 🔁 for it, matching the Always button Telegram and Lark already offer. The allowance is session-scoped, the same grant the typed reply makes. 🔁 sits between ✅ and ❌ so it is not the first or last reaction under the prompt.
  - Reactions use the typed path's authorization: the peer allowlist, `allowed_rooms`, the prompt's own room, and first decision wins. Matrix keeps its approvals in one private state in `matrix.rs`: live registrations, each with its prompt's event ID, plus the 64 most recently settled tokens. Resolution, timeout and cancellation retire a registration and its binding together, so a late tap does nothing.
  - A typed reply to one of those recently settled tokens is consumed instead of reaching the agent as ordinary chat. Without this, tapping ✅ and then typing `<TOKEN> always` sent the protocol text into a model turn. Older or unknown token-shaped text keeps its existing behaviour.
  - Reaction seeding runs alongside the wait for a decision. A slow or failing `/send/m.reaction` only logs at `WARN`; it never delays a typed answer or stretches `approval_timeout_secs`.
  - The homeserver can show the prompt before the bot learns its event ID, so a tap in that gap reaches sync before there is a binding. After binding, the bot reads the prompt's existing `m.annotation` relations, newest first, and runs each through the same decision path as a live reaction, so an early tap still counts. This runs alongside seeding, adds no state, and a failure only logs at `WARN`.
  - When the bot can seed reactions, the prompt shows only the reaction instruction. Typed replies with the token from the heading still work, for clients and bridges that cannot react, replies from a notification, and seeding failures. Without a bot identity, the prompt keeps the typed instruction.
  - `Cargo.lock` moves `pulldown-cmark` from 0.13.5 to 0.13.6 for RUSTSEC-2026-0433, which failed the Security check. @IftekharUddin proposed the same update.
  - A tap on a live prompt that fails authorization logs at `INFO` with the sender, room, prompt event and reason. Reactions that are not approval answers stay unlogged.
- **Scope boundary:** Apart from the `pulldown-cmark` lock update, typed reply parsing, approval routing and the runtime's approval policy are unchanged. No other channel's behaviour changes.
- **Blast radius:** Matrix only. The Discord, Signal, Slack and Telegram sources are unchanged. `crates/zeroclaw-channels/src/util.rs` changes only by dropping `channel-matrix` from the `cfg` lists of the shared approval-map helpers, which Matrix no longer uses. Each Matrix registration carries an identity, so a stale guard or delayed send cannot touch a later registration that reuses the same token.
- **Linked issue(s):** None. Related #10358 (Mattermost approval prompts).

### What this does, simply

When ZeroClaw needs permission to run a tool, it asks in the Matrix room. Until now, the operator had to copy a code from the message and type it back with "approve" or "deny". With this change, the bot puts ✅, 🔁 and ❌ under its own question, and the operator taps one: ✅ approves this call, 🔁 approves this tool for the rest of the session, and ❌ denies it. Only the same people who could type an answer can tap one, and the tap must be in the same room. Typing still works.

## Testing (required)

### How you can test (when useful)

- **Reviewer testing requested?** Yes. CI cannot cover a live homeserver or a real client.
- **Interface(s) exercised:** `channel` = `matrix`.
- **Setup / preconditions:** A Matrix channel alias with a peer group containing your account, in an encrypted room, and a risk profile that asks for some tool.
- **Steps to run:** Ask the agent to use that tool, tap ✅ on the prompt, and repeat with 🔁 and ❌. Then react with another emoji, tap from an account outside the peer group, and tap after the prompt has been answered.
- **Expected on this branch (after):** The prompt carries ✅, 🔁 and ❌. Tapping ✅ runs the call once, 🔁 runs it and skips the prompt for that tool for the rest of the session, ❌ denies it, and other emoji, outsiders and late taps do nothing. Typed replies still work.
- **Prior behavior on `master` (before):** The prompt has no reactions, and only typed replies answer it.

### How I tested

- **CI checks relied on and why they cover this change:** The Rust test, clippy and fmt jobs cover `zeroclaw-channels`.
- **Known CI coverage gap, if any:** No test runs against a live homeserver or Element.
- **Commands run and tail output:**

```text
$ cargo fmt --all -- --check
(no output)

$ cargo test -p zeroclaw-channels --no-default-features --features channel-matrix --lib matrix
test result: ok. 327 passed; 0 failed; 3 ignored; 0 measured; 870 filtered out

$ cargo test -p zeroclaw-channels --lib
test result: ok. 2031 passed; 0 failed; 2 ignored; 0 measured; 0 filtered out

$ cargo +1.98.0 clippy -p zeroclaw-channels --all-targets -- -D warnings
Finished `dev` profile [unoptimized + debuginfo] target(s)

$ cargo run -p xtask --bin fluent -- check
(exit 0)
```

  Before this change the Matrix filter reported 313 passed. With `--no-default-features --features channel-matrix`, clippy reports `function manager_from_snapshot is never used` on both `master` and this branch, so that finding predates this change.
- **Beyond CI, what did you manually verify?** New tests drive real matrix-sdk 0.19.1 sync dispatch through `MatrixMockServer`. prs.title: fix(tools): let glob_search list files under read-only and outside roots
prs.body:
## Summary

- **Base branch:** `master`
- **What changed and why:**
  - `glob_search` accepts absolute patterns under any readable root (read-write or read-only) instead of only read-write/write-only roots, so `workspace.access` read grants work like they do for `file_read`.
  - Matches outside the workspace are returned with their absolute path instead of being silently dropped by the workspace-relative conversion. This completes the intent of #3434 (closes #3082), which allowed such patterns at the pre-check but left the result filter workspace-only.
  - Tool description (code and English Fluent catalogues) and the tools overview now say that absolute patterns under an allowed root are supported, so models know they can use them.
- **Scope boundary:** no change to path policy, readability checks, symlink handling or other tools; non-English catalogues are left to the localization workflow.
- **Blast radius:** `glob_search` output only. Workspace matches keep their relative form; outside matches were previously never returned.
- **Linked issue(s):** Closes #12225. Related #3082, #3434.

### What this does, simply

An agent can be allowed to read folders outside its own working directory. Reading and searching inside those folders already worked, but listing their files with `glob_search` always came back empty, and folders shared read-only from another agent were refused outright. This PR makes `glob_search` behave like `file_read` and `content_search`: if a folder is readable, its files can be listed. Write-only folders still never appear, because each match is still checked for readability.

## Testing (required)

### How you can test (when useful)

- **Reviewer testing requested?** N/A: covered by the new unit tests; the A/B output on `master` is below.

### How I tested

- **CI checks relied on and why they cover this change:** Rust tests and the workspace clippy job (`scripts/ci/run_clippy.sh`, toolchain 1.98.0) cover `zeroclaw-tools`; the English Fluent catalogue change is covered by the i18n catalogue tests.

test result: ok. 1384 passed; 0 failed; 3 ignored; 0 measured; 0 filtered out

New tests:
